title: Boat of the month: F/V Judy S pursues tuna - Chinook Observer
content: Captain: Walker Kellogg, 35Vessel: F/V Judy SBuilder: Martin AllenYear built: 1975Home port: IlwacoLength: 53 feetHull: Steel Can you tell me a little about the boat and what you fish for? “The boat used to fish the South Pacific tuna season, and now it fishes the North Pacific tuna season,” said F/V Judy S skipper Walker Kellogg, 35, of Winchester Bay, Oregon, after returning to the Port of Ilwaco on Saturday, Nov. 7, following his final commercial albacore trip of the season. “It’s a high-producing, super-solid offshore platform. It’s a steel boat that’s been around a long time. We primarily crab and fish for tuna.” “I’ve been full time since I was 18. I ran this boat last year for tuna season and have since taken it over as a full-time operator. I just chase the seasons. Crab is coming next, followed by salmon, black cod and tuna. I’ll mainly participate in crab and tuna, then work some other things in.” “Pretty decent. Fuel prices were high. That definitely played a part in a lot of guys’ strategies.” “We’re looking for a core temperature of about -30 degrees Celsius [minus-22 degrees Fahrenheit]. It’s -35 in there right now.” Thank you for reading the Chinook Observer.Subscribe to get Unlimited Access to our website.

title: Evaluating Jonathan Taylor's workload v. Cowboys before trade deadline - Yahoo Sports
content: Although it's possible that Jonathan Taylor could end up being traded before Tuesday's 4:00 PM ET deadline, the Indianapolis Colts continue to play him. So what did his workload look like against the Dallas Cowboys? According to PFF, the Colts ran 64 offensive plays on Sunday, and Taylor was out there for 44 of them -- a good amount. He finished the game with 18 total touches, 13 of which came as a ball carrier. It was tough sledding for Taylor on the ground, who again averaged under 4.0 yards per attempt. He also fumbled as well, which potentially took points off the board late. As a pass-catcher, Taylor's five receptions went for only 18 yards. While Taylor has been at the center of trade speculation, it remains to be seen if he will be dealt. The Ringer's Tom Pelissero reported on Saturday that the "most likely destination" for Taylor is staying in Indianapolis. Jay Glazer reported that the Giants' offer for Taylor, which included a second-round pick, is "off the table." This article originally appeared on Colts Wire: Evaluating Jonathan Taylor's workload v. Cowboys before trade deadline

title: Why Cadillac's V-Series EVs Can't Hot-Lap Yet - Yahoo Autos
content: Cadillac slaps the V-Series badge on its electric cars, but the brand will tell you plainly that those cars are not built to run a race track lap after lap. The holdup is heat. The battery pack and electric motors throw off excess warmth that keeps building the longer you drive hard, and once it crosses a threshold, the car scales back power to protect itself. That is fine for a canyon road. It is a problem on a circuit, where the second lap needs to be as quick as the first. Cadillac vehicle performance engineer Tom Schinderle, who works on the gasoline CT5-V Blackwing, put the current state of the EV program in blunt terms. The electric V-Series cars are tuned for "canyon carving, spirited driving," not full track performance. The company has even built track-capable electric concepts internally, but it will not badge them or sell them until they clear GM's own durability bar. Pushed hard, a battery and a set of motors heat up, and hot cells cannot deliver their rated output. Schinderle identified thermal management as the main obstacle keeping Cadillac's electric performance models from meeting GM's internal standards. In performance EVs broadly, heat that builds up in the pack and drive units tends to throttle output after a single fast lap. This is not a theoretical concern buried in an engineer's spreadsheet. GM documents the behavior for owners. When the high-voltage battery pack runs beyond its ideal temperature window in either direction, it may fall short of the power output expected of it, and the car responds with messages like "Reduced Acceleration, Drive with Care" and "Propulsion Power Reduced Due to Temperature." The state of charge at which power gets throttled shifts with battery temperature. At a moderate pack temperature around 68 degrees F, reduced propulsion typically shows up only down near 5 percent to 10 percent charge. Get the pack very warm, though, such as right after a fast charge in extreme ambient heat, and reduced propulsion can arrive at any state of charge. So the car protects itself by cutting power when it overheats. That is exactly the wrong trait for a track toy, where overheating is the baseline condition rather than the exception. A spirited run up a mountain road involves bursts of hard acceleration followed by braking and coasting, which gives the cooling system room to catch up. A track lap removes those breaks. You are at or near full commitment for a sustained stretch, repeatedly, with no highway cruise to let temperatures settle. Schinderle framed the goal as building a car that can do it "lap after lap after lap," and that phrase is the dividing line between a quick road car and a real track machine. Cadillac is not willing to call something track-capable until it can sustain performance across repeated laps rather than fading after the first. Cadillac's current benchmark for track endurance is not electric at all. The car that holds up best on track is the CT5-V Blackwing, powered by a supercharged 6.2-liter V8 rated at 668 horsepower and 659 pound-feet of torque. It even offers a Precision Package built specifically to sharpen track behavior. Schinderle pointed to those combustion sedans as proof of what Cadillac expects. He told CarExpert that the V-Series ICE sedans can run "lap after lap after lap," and that the company is investigating the same for its EVs but is "just not quite ready to commit to that yet." Some of the holdup is self-imposed. Cadillac says it already has electric concepts that can take on a race track, but those concepts have not "passed all of our internal benchmarks that are critically important." Schinderle credited GM's internal rules for the gap, saying the company holds itself to durability standards "stricter than our counterparts and our competitors." This is not the first time a Cadillac engineer has named the culprit. Lyriq-V lead development engineer Alex Doss has made the same case before, naming battery weight and cooling as the big obstacles to a Blackwing-badged EV. Two engineers, same conclusion: the electrons are fast, the thermal plumbing is not there yet. Today's V-Series EVs are not without a track-flavored setting. They include a Competitive Mode that, in Schinderle's words, backs out traction control "ever so slightly" and shifts the front-to-rear power split toward the rear so the car can step out on corner exit. He described the result as making the car more agile "just on a corner exit." That is a handling tweak, not an endurance solution. It changes how the car behaves in a corner. It does nothing about the heat that forces a power cut on lap two. The feature owners might actually want for the track, a layered traction system, is still on the wish list. Schinderle suggested a progressive traction management system comparable to the one on the ICE Blackwing could eventually reach the EVs, but only once a Cadillac EV is signed off as capable of repeated hot-lapping. His phrasing was conditional: when the cars get to that point, "that's when the progressive traction control would make it." Thermal first, then the software. If you push one of these cars hard and watch the power fade, you are not looking at a broken car. GM classifies the "Reduced Acceleration," "Drive with Care," and "Propulsion Power Reduced Due to Temperature" messages, along with the limited power that comes with them, as normal operating responses when battery power is limited by charge or temperature. The behavior spans much of GM's EV range, not just Cadillac, including the Lyriq, Optiq, Celestiq, and Escalade IQ as well as the Hummer EV, Silverado EV, Sierra EV, and Blazer EV. Tellingly, the condition sets no propulsion-related diagnostic trouble codes, even though a propulsion-limited warning light may come on. There is nothing to fix because nothing is wrong. The car is doing what it was programmed to do. If you drive a V-Series EV and want to enjoy it, keep its limits in mind rather than fighting them. In hot weather, GM recommends reducing cabin cooling so the system can divert more cooling to the battery when the pack is at 20 percent charge or higher. In the cold, keeping the car plugged in after a full charge helps maintain pack temperature for the next drive. These steps smooth out the power-limiting behavior in daily use, but they will not turn a canyon car into a track car. For actual circuit duty, the honest answer today is the gasoline CT5-V Blackwing, with a next-generation version expected down the road. Cadillac's electric performance cars are quick in a straight line and lively on a back road, and the brand is clearly working the thermal problem. Just do not buy one expecting it to survive a track day session without pulling its punches. When Cadillac is confident an EV can hold up lap after lap, it will say so, and the progressive traction tools will follow. Until then, the V badge on an electric Cadillac is a promise about the road, not the paddock. Become a TTAC insider. title: England v Wallabies: Five takeaways as 'un-Australian performance' fails to dampen 'sparkler' of an English showing from key man - Planet Rugby
content: England v Wallabies: Five takeaways as 'un-Australian performance' fails to dampen 'sparkler' of an English performance from key man England posted their highest-ever score against Australia in a seven-try 45-22 annihilation of the Wallabies at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham, and here are our five takeaways. Twickenham served up a grey and murky afternoon and, for the best part of an hour, grey and murky rugby to go with the skies above it, but in the final analysis England put seven tries past the Wallabies in a 45-22 win that’s their highest score ever posted against Australia and just one point short of the record winning margin against them. We really have to give Steve Borthwick and England their due. They started slowly and at times were every bit as inaccurate as Australia in that opening quarter, but they maintained discipline, they maintained focus and concentration, they kept 15 men on the pitch and, the longer the game went on, so the stronger and more impressive England became. The press has criticised Borthwick roundly for his data-driven approach this week, but what he’s shown today is the ability to use that data and insight to make his team better, and that shouldn’t be lost in all the drudgery. Maybe this isn’t the Galacticos and the glitterati, but what it is, is a thunderingly intelligent and professional display that’s solid, glue-like and mature, if some way from being the final polished article. Let’s be honest, this wasn’t a game played by a side that were unhappy in camp, short of structure or short of discipline, which is quite a statement after some of the things that have been written. There are many elements of the press that gave England a hell of a pep talk this week. Let’s start with the stick England have been beaten with, 14 yellow cards and a red in eight matches. Today they had none, they conceded only seven penalties to Australia’s 11, and the difference that made was clearly seen on the scoreboard. Twice an Australian offence went straight to the corner and came back as five points. Jack van Poortvliet’s poor kick was fielded easily enough on seven minutes, only for Australia to give it all back with an obstruction in the air, and Jamie George was driven over from the maul; then, on 31 minutes, Angus Bell went in with a hip-drop on Manny Feyi-Waboso, and it’s hard to understand how players still can’t tackle in any other way. A minute later, Joe Heyes was over from the next maul and Australia were 19-3 down with 14 men. Although the bunker left it at yellow, the cost to England went beyond 10 minutes, as Feyi-Waboso limped from there on and never came back out for the second half. Underneath that sat a defensive performance of real substance. England made 81 tackles in the first half and missed only two, using a defensive system that went 13-2, but with Feyi-Waboso also back whenever the kick was obvious, a clever hybrid that kept numbers in the line and still left cover for the boot. They were really physical on the one and two runners, which is where Australia’s game never really fired. Unfortunately, as the game broke up, they missed 17 more after the break, but as Australia looked to play catch-up, with the result long settled, Henry Slade and Henry Pollock found a way to stop a certain try in the corner on 73 minutes, a microcosm of the change in attitude since last year. Maro Itoje led the way with 17 tackles and two turnovers, and whilst Slade’s player of the match award might have been slightly odd, the guy didn’t put a foot wrong. England won 94 per cent of their own lineout, with Ollie Chessum stealing Australian ball three times, and Fin Baxter and Heyes were both strong, despite one penalty for chasing the hit. England player ratings v Australia: Henry Pollock-led Pom Squad returns in ‘lethal fashion’ amid ‘big mister efforts’ from the pack England showed us what they’ve been working on in training almost straight away. With play switching quickly from left to right, Chessum was seen stationed on the left wing, with Feyi-Waboso coming in off it into the 13 channel at pace, and he was over inside two minutes, only for Ben Curry’s clearly forward pass in the build-up to chalk it off. But it was a portent of things to come. They returned to the same move on 25 minutes. Feyi-Waboso was popping up all over the place at 12 and 13, but crucially Chessum held his spot out wide. England cut back through a mazy Feyi-Waboso run and, when the ball reached George Furbank, there were two more attackers than defenders on that side, with Chessum left only to take the pass and score. Lee Blackett, England’s attack coach, used to do exactly this at Wasps with Brad Shields and Tom Willis, and it’s really clever stuff; you bring your winger back infield, you leave your forward on the touchline and the defence has to work out who’s marking who with the ball already moving, but leaving you with power should you need to crash it up on the wing. Feyi-Waboso was the sparkler in all of this; for 40 minutes it was 29 men and Manny. He finished with 113 running metres, seven defenders beaten and two clean breaks from one half of rugby, and nobody else on the pitch matched those metres or that number of defenders beaten. Losing him might have finished the plan, but England simply found an extra man from somewhere else. Furbank, in his first Test since November 2024, came into the line two minutes into the half, threw a magnificent dummy and passed outside to Tommy Freeman, who threw it back inside to Van Poortvliet, running a lovely line to finish a stormer of a try, and Furbank ended the day with two try assists. Then there was the gamble. Borthwick sent the peroxide Pom Henry Pollock to the wing at half-time, with only Ben Spencer and Marcus Smith left as backs on the 6-2 bench. He could have handed the press a loaded revolver with which to shoot him when he made the statement about Pollock as a utility back but, let’s be honest, he’s absolutely nailed this one. Mind you, Borthwick has been talking about Pollock as a wing for a year, so this was planned for, and it showed. On 54 minutes, with Australia under pressure on their own line, the ball came loose and Pollock swept it up and went over; the boy loves a try. Two minutes later he took the final pass from another Furbank and Freeman move and went 25 metres to finish like a flying wing. England’s replacements scored three of the seven tries, with Spencer barely on the field for a minute before he went flying down the wing. Opinion: Average All Blacks blunder on and why someone other than the Springboks will expose them Credit England, but this was such an un-Australian performance, with no ambition, no handling and not enough athleticism from a side that beat South Africa 42-38 only six weeks ago in Perth. Les Kiss made a big call in starting Josh Canham and Lukhan Salakaia-Loto together, shifting Jeremy Williams to six and Rob Valetini to the bench, and it brought him very little. Australia won a miserly 75 per cent of their lineout and, when Valetini arrived on 46 minutes and Taniela Tupou a minute later, England went on to win the critical 50-70 minute window 12-5. Australia were decent in the air, with Tom Wright and his wings sharing that contest, but they killed themselves with error after error, trying to run the ball out of their own half on a number of occasions. The backline was absolutely dreadful; it was as if Les Kiss had walked into the Walkabout at Shepherd’s Bush and asked the drinkers who was available for the afternoon. Their one moment of fortune came on 39 minutes, when Van Poortvliet’s lazy, lolloping pass was picked off by Max Jorgensen for a 61-metre try they didn’t deserve. That’s the issue with the England nine; his backlift and load-up take so long that sometimes his passing is telegraphed. But to be fair to him, he made 59 passes, ran a superb line for his try three minutes later and finished the day on the winning side. England took five of our six measures, winning the kick metres 355 to 312 and the carry metres 576 to 339, conceding fewer turnovers, 15 to 19, and fewer penalties, seven to 11, and making 14 entries into the Australian 22 to two; only the rucks went Australia’s way, 74 to 79. A bonus-point win takes England to 15 points, level with Ireland and 42 better off on points difference, with Japan and then New Zealand to come at Twickenham before Finals Weekend, and there’s the rub, because Australia were woeful today and you’re only as good as your opponent lets you be. New Zealand won’t be so generous, and England will want good news on Feyi-Waboso’s fitness long before then. But for now that’s seven tries, no cards, the highest score England have ever put past Australia and two fingers up to certain parts of the press and their unwarranted criticisms. title: Colts WR Ashton Dulin provides needed big play touchdown v. Cowboys - Yahoo Sports
content: The Indianapolis Colts have struggled to generate explosive plays on offense throughout this season. However, they scored a long touchdown against the Cowboys to make it 20-17 Dallas in the fourth quarter. Quarterback Daniel Jones threw a screen pass to receiver Ashton Dulin, who broke multiple tackles and turned on the speed to take it 55 yards to the end zone for a touchdown. It was Dulin's first touchdown since 2024, and he only had three catches all year before this play. Here is a look at Dulin's touchdown, courtesy of the Indianapolis Colts' official social media: That score was the first touchdown pass for Jones that was over 10 yards this season as well as his longest touchdown pass since joining the Colts. It was also just the third touchdown for Indianapolis this season of at least 10 yards; the previous two were touchdown runs from Jonathan Taylor. After Dulin's touchdown, the Colts defense was able to force their second turnover of the game, giving Indianapolis' offense the chance to take their first lead since 14:09 was left in the second quarter. title: Uganda win Women’s IHF Nations Trophy – Africa Zone V in dramatic fashion - IHF
content:
Uganda won the Women’s IHF Nations Trophy – Africa Zone V with a 29:28 win over Kenya in the final, settled by a Joyce Namutosi goal 74 seconds from the end. The competition was played from 4 to 8 November at the Filbert Bayi Multi Sports Center in Kibaha, Tanzania. Six teams took part in the competition, split into two groups of three. Kenya, Uganda and Ethiopia played in Group A, while hosts Tanzania, Rwanda and Djibouti made up Group B. The top two teams in each group advanced to the semi-finals, and the third-placed sides met in the match for fifth place. Uganda opened the competition on 4 November with a 45:18 win against Ethiopia. The match was level at 10:10 after 18 minutes, but Uganda then scored 14 goals in a row to lead 24:10 at half-time, and added a 10:0 run in the second half, from 30:16 to 40:16. Royce Namutosi scored 12 goals and Tiane Nakirya 11, the only two performances of more than ten goals in a single match at the competition. In the second match of the day, Tanzania beat Djibouti 54:14 after leading 19:6 at the break. The hosts put together four long scoring runs: 10:0 from 6:2 to 16:2, 8:0 from 27:10 to 35:10, 6:0 from 37:12 to 43:12, and 11:0 in the last six minutes, from 43:14 to the final score. Amina Dauda scored ten goals for Tanzania. On the second day, Kenya beat Ethiopia 41:6. Ethiopia did not score in the first half, which ended 18:0, and Kenya’s opening run reached 20:0 before Ethiopia found the net early in the second half. Kenya then scored 17 goals in a row, from 20:3 to 37:3. Rwanda beat Djibouti 49:9 after leading 25:3 at half-time. They started with a 9:0 run, added a 6:0 run from 9:1 to 15:1, and scored 19 unanswered goals. Kenya topped Group A with a 30:27 win against Uganda. They trailed 3:4 after nine minutes, then scored eight goals in a row to lead 11:4, and were 15:9 ahead at half-time. Uganda won the second half 18:15, but could not close the gap. In Group B, Rwanda beat Tanzania 42:32 after leading 21:13 at the break, with Obadia Niyingenera scoring ten for Rwanda and Dauda another ten for Tanzania. The semi-finals were played on 7 November. Kenya beat Tanzania 36:22 after leading 20:6 at half-time. The second semi-final needed extra time. Rwanda scored six goals in a row, from 6:9 to 12:9, and led Uganda 17:11 at the break. Uganda won the second half 20:14, and the closing minutes swung both ways. Joyce Namutosi levelled at 30:30 in the 59th minute, Clementine Hungurimana restored Rwanda’s lead at 31:30, and Royce Namutosi equalised 14 seconds later to force extra time. Uganda won the first period of extra time 3:1 and held on to win 37:35.

The bronze medal match on 8 November also turned late. Rwanda led Tanzania 29:23 after 46 minutes, before the hosts scored seven unanswered goals and went ahead 30:29 through Monicah Mpanda Joseph in the 56th minute. Clesence Irakoze equalised, and Hungurimana scored twice in the last 90 seconds, the second 13 seconds before the end, to give Rwanda a 32:31 win. Kenya and Uganda met again in the final, three days after Kenya’s group-stage win. The score was level ten times, and neither team managed a run of more than four goals. Cecilia Katheu Kiio gave Kenya the lead, before Uganda replied with four goals in a row from Hilda Abangit, Claire Tabingwa, Tiane Nakirya and Patience Damulira, and Damulira’s second goal made it 1:5 after five and a half minutes. Kenya answered with four straight goals of their own to draw level at 6:6 in the 13th minute, and Merina Andala put them 10:9 ahead in the 20th minute. Uganda scored twice in the final minutes of the half to lead 13:12 at the break. Uganda moved three goals clear at 18:15 in the 39th minute and kept that margin until 22:19. Kenya then scored three in a row through Melvin Akinyi, Gail Eucabeth Opar and Elizabeth Achieng to level at 22:22 in the 47th minute. Uganda went two ahead again at 25:23 and 26:24, but Kenya came back to 26:26 in the 55th minute, and Akinyi gave them a 27:26 lead with 3:20 to play. Diana Nakamya replied with two goals in 16 seconds to put Uganda 28:27 ahead, Martha Lavender Muyekho levelled at 28:28 in the 58th minute, and Joyce Namutosi scored the winner with 74 seconds left. Joyce Namutosi and Muyekho each scored seven goals in the final, with Nakamya and Nakirya adding five each for Uganda. Uganda finished first ahead of Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Ethiopia and Djibouti. Rwanda’s Obadia Niyingenera and Uganda’s Royce Namutosi shared the top-scorer title with 30 goals each, followed by Rwanda’s Clementine Hungurimana with 29 and Tanzania’s Zawadi Athumani with 26. Tanzania’s Amina Dauda and Kenya’s Martha Lavender Muyekho scored 25 each.

With their win, Uganda qualified for the 2026 CAHB African Women's Handball Championship. By continuing to browse ihf.info, you agree to our terms of use , privacy policy and the use of cookies. For more information, please review our cookie policy.

title: Man Utd claw back draw with stoppage-time goals v Villa - RTE.ie
content:
Patrick Dorgu secured Manchester United a scarcely believable 4-4 draw deep into stoppage time as under-fire Michael Carrick denied Aston Villa amid a backdrop of anger against the club's ownership. Old Trafford witnessed an astonishing helter-skelter encounter on Sunday afternoon as the embattled, and deeply flawed, Red Devils showed spirit against the odds as they had against Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday. United again fell two goals behind as Alysson and Nicolas Jackson capitalised on wretched play inside four minutes as supporters called for the Glazers and United co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe to sell up. Bruno Fernandes pulled one back from the spot, just like in the 3-2 Champions League comeback victory against Roma, and Youri Tielemans equalised against his former club just before half-time. But renewed United hope was dented at the start of the second half, with John McGinn scoring a penalty gifted to Villa by Diogo Dalot – whose substitution would be brutally cheered – before Leon Goretzka added another. They were the latest self-inflicted wounds in a season of gaffes by Carrick’s side but the players fought until the death, with substitute Joshua Zirkzee reducing the deficit in stoppage time before fellow substitute Dorgu sparked bedlam. Quite whether it is enough to keep the United head coach in the job is another matter, though, with the side to spend the November international break in 18th place. The change fans really want goes far beyond the man in the dugout, as highlighted by the green and gold balloons that filled the air around a banner that read 'we don't want a new stadium, we want new owners’. The furious chants against the Glazers, Ratcliffe and director of football Jason Wilcox went up a notch after Unai Emery’s men capitalised on hodgepodge defending in the first minute. The ball was played wide for Alysson and Dalot allowed him space to hit a first-time strike through Senne Lammens’ legs. The mood darkened further in the fourth minute. United failed to deal with a free-kick and Alysson’s strike was spilled by Lammens, with Jackson sweeping the ball into an empty net. "You’re not fit to wear the shirt" bellowed home fans as Villa teased Carrick about his job prospects, only for Tuesday’s matchwinner Matheus Cunha to draw a foul from Boubacar Kamara in the box. Fernandes scored after the VAR ratified the on-field call, with the 16th-minute penalty sparking the best Premier League display from United since their solitary domestic win back in August. Zion Suzuki brilliantly stopped a curling Cunha effort shortly after a mooted walkout failed to materialise, with Fernandes twice trying his luck as Kobbie Mainoo and Amad Diallo threatened. Amad continued to prove a nuisance and United’s hard work was rewarded just before half-time. Tielemans’ low strike from just inside the box beat Suzuki, whose appeals that his view was impeded by Bryan Mbeumo were immaterial as the forward was onside. But belief there could be a comeback like against Roma did not last long. Dalot’s sloppy challenge on Alysson gave Villa a penalty that McGinn coolly slotted home three minutes into the second half. United failed to steady the ship and in the 54th minute Leny Yoro’s attempt to deal with a free-kick sent the ball flying towards his own goal. Lammens tipped it onto the crossbar but Goretzka was able to eventually prod home. The quickfire double rocked United as Cunha and Mbeumo had efforts in their attempts to drag themselves off the canvas. A huge cheer greeted Dalot’s substitution and Old Trafford would empty as the clock wound down, only for those that stayed to be rewarded with a dramatic conclusion. Mason Mount hit the crossbar and fellow sub Zirkzee pulled one back in stoppage time when turning home a Dorgu cross. Those remaining roared on the team and the sixth minute of stoppage time brought bedlam. Dorgu rose to head home a Fernandes corner, with Suzuki’s appeals he was upended trying to meet the cross ignored. Under-fire Carrick left applauding fans chanting his name at the end of a crazy game. © RTÉ 2026. RTÉ.ie is the website of Raidió Teilifís Éireann, Ireland's National Public Service Media. title: Dorgu makes dramatic impact - Man Utd v Aston Villa ratings - BBC
content: Patrick Dorgu rises to head Manchester United's injury-time equaliser in a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa Manchester United fought back from two goals twice to draw 4-4 with Aston Villa as Patrick Dorgu made a dramatic impact off the bench. But who impressed and who didn't in the Old Trafford epic? Senne Lammens: One of Man Utd's best performers this season but a calamitous start to this one. First goal went straight through him and he spilled a shot straight from Nicolas Jackson for the second. Went wrong way for penalty too. 4 Diogo Dalot (off 66, Dorgu): Got his body in the right position to close half the goal off for the opener but was in the wrong position to make challenge on Alysson at start of second half to gift Villa a penalty. 4 Leny Yoro: Moved back into the centre, intelligently stepped up to win the ball on halfway, then spoiled good work by attempting a lofted pass when Matheus Cunha wanted it on the ground. Almost headed into his own net in build-up to Villa's fourth goal. 5 Harry Maguire (off 46, Heaven): Managed to clear his head quickly enough to lead United's defence after their shocking start. A doubt pre-match, he went off at half-time. 5 Noussair Mazraoui: Struggled along with many others this season. Asked to push forward, which he seems to find easier for his country but not his club. 4 Youri Tielemans (off 66, Mount): Baited by the Aston Villa fans given his £35m summer move from them, but answered in the best way by driving home an equaliser for his first United goal. 6 Kobbie Mainoo: Threatened with a long-range effort and nearly picked out Amad Diallo's run with a precise chipped pass over the visitors defence. 6 Amad Diallo (off 66, Lacey): Kept his place ahead of crowd favourite Shea Lacey but one chase back into his own box showed why, defensively, it made sense. Came close to an equaliser and should have ended an 11-month wait for a goal but Zion Suzuki saved well. 6 Bruno Fernandes: For the second game running, he kept his cool to covert from the spot when the pressure was at its highest. Looked unhappy at the end despite the comeback. 7 Matheus Cunha: Driving run into the visiting box brought a crucial penalty. Curling effort was heading for the corner but turned around post by Suzuki. United's most dangerous attacker. 7 Bryan Mbeumo (off 83, Zirkzee): Did a lot of chasing in the first half to try to pressure the Villa defence into mistakes. 6 Ayden Heaven (on 46, Maguire): Booked for late tackle on Alysson after being introduced at break. 6 Mason Mount (on 66, Tielemans): Hit the bar with first time shot but sliced later effort over. 6 Patrick Dorgu (on 66 Dalot): What an ending as he changed the outcome of the game with an assist and goal. 8 Joshua Zirkzee (on 83, Mbeumo): Scored in stoppage time and goal proved crucial. 6 Subs not used: Darlow, De Ligt, Andrey Santos, J Fletcher. Bizarre & thrilling theatre as Carrick's Man Utd future still in limbo Premier League: Man Utd score twice in stoppage time to draw with Villa but stay in drop zone Zion Suzuki: Kept busy as the hosts hunted an equaliser. One excellent save from Cunha and a couple when he benefited from a kind rebound, but bad error for United's late equaliser. 5 Victor Lindelof: Found himself under a lot of pressure on a ground he knows so well and turned in an accomplished performance. 7 Taylor Harwood-Bellis: Had to remain concentrated and wasn't faultless but emerged with credit in the bank. 6 Pau Torres: Guided a header over as Villa attacked but biggest task was trying to stop Cunha. As it turned out, a stride too late getting out when Tielemans scored. Couldn't keep United out in the end. 6 Ian Maatsen: Testing day, trying to stop Amad attacking and looking to beat Mazraoui at the other end. Was doing well until the late drama. 7 Alysson (off 71, Barkley): Even the Brazilian must have been a little bit surprised his first-minute shot ended up in the net. His shot created the second and came so close to adding another to his tally after being released by Goretzka. Won the penalty at start of second half too. 8 Boubacar Kamara: Ill-advised attempted tackle on Cunha led to penalty that offered the hosts a way back into the game. Struggled to contain the home attack. 7 John McGinn (off 71, Hemmings): Everything looked so good in the opening minutes but then had to try to ensure Villa didn't fall apart as United fought back. Kept his concentration to score from the spot and created panic with a free-kick. 7 Leon Goretzka (off 78, Mbaye): Tried to relieve pressure on Villa defence as the hosts fought back and drove home Villa's fourth on a crazy day. 7 Johan Manzambi (off 78, Gomes): Not the easiest game for the Swiss international to shine given its general chaotic nature. Tried to get control but no real chance of that. 5 Nicolas Jackson (off 86, Madjo): Alert to snaffle home the rebound after Lammens had spilled McGinn's shot. Not the best performance but much effective than in his Chelsea days. 7 George Hemmings (on 71, McGinn): Came on to shore things up but move didn't work. 5 Ross Barkley (on 71, Alysson): Won't remember ending with fondness. 5 After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: England v Australia: Winners and losers as Henry Pollock 'continues to back it up' but Immanuel Feyi-Waboso exit raises concerns - Planet Rugby
content: England v Australia: Winners and losers as Henry Pollock 'continues to back it up' but Immanuel Feyi-Waboso exit raises concerns England defeated the Wallabies 45-22 at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham, on Sunday evening in round four of the Nations Championship. Interviewed by Sky Sports during the week, the former England captain expressed his “hurt” at having to deal with a Times article attacking head coach Steve Borthwick two days before the match. He said that the accusations presented in said article would only “galvanise” his side, and he wasn’t wrong. The experienced hooker opened the scoring to become the top-scoring England forward in history. With just 12 months left as an international rugby player, he put in an industrious defensive performance of which he will be proud. It was his first England appearance since playing France at the end of the disastrous 2026 Six Nations campaign. After taking the summer off, he’s returned fresh and firing. Recently named Saracens’ player of the month, he continued his rich vein of form on Sunday, making an incredible 17 tackles and throwing himself into every facet of the game. This looked like a truly rejuvenated Maro Itoje. Another who hasn’t been seen in an England shirt for quite some time, the now-Harlequins man returned after two years away from international rugby after being forced to contend with a series of unfortunate injuries. The fit-again playmaker was excellent at full-back, showing terrific passing abilities and a running game, which once made him a firm favourite in Steve Borthwick’s side. There were concerns that the Northampton Saints fly-half would not return to fitness ahead of this game, but he showed no signs of rustiness after shaking off a recent calf injury. His gainline skills were matched only by his physicality in the contact area, as he once again proved that he is growing into a genuine all-around world-class talent. Death, taxes and Henry Pollock making the headlines: all things that are inevitable in life. The young Saints star appeared in the unconventional position of wing on Sunday, but the results followed a familiar pattern – two tries, two celebrations, and a whole lot of hysteria over this thrilling character. He has a lot to say, and certainly attracts a whole orchestra of attention, but the key fact is that he continues to back it up. Wales player ratings v Japan: Louis Rees-Zammit ‘leads the way’ in hard-fought win over spirited Brave Blossoms Just when England threatened to turn the screw on the Wallabies, the loosehead prop dropped his hip in the tackle and was punished with a sin-bin dismissal. Joe Hayes subsequently went over from the resulting penalty, and England started to take real control of the match. Fortunately for Bell, teammate Max Jorgensen flew over for a try against the run of play just before the break, as England failed to fully make the one-man advantage pay. With a display like that, how could he possibly be a loser? Injury, of course. Sadly, the Exeter Chiefs winger failed to return to the field for the second-half, after suffering an injury in the tackle by Angus Bell. He looked in serious discomfort but powered on to half-time, when presumably a consultation with a physio and a discussion by the higher-ups suggested that his day was over. Although sad for Feyi-Waboso, his opponents would have taken a deep sigh of relief after the speedster had demolished their defence, beating an average of one defender with each carry and making 130 metres with the ball in hand. It is genuinely remarkable how under the radar the Gloucester Rugby man seems, despite never appearing to have a bad game. But then again, that might be why he’s so under the radar; he never gives a reason to attract attention, wanted or not. His defence was solid; he linked well with those around him, and generally kept the Wallabies’ attack in his pocket, but he does appear to lack the magic that international players require. Again, however, the reason for his loser tag is that he hobbled off with a quarter of the game remaining. His injury could cast doubt over his ownership of the 12 shirt, with the likes of Max Ojomoh and Fraser Dingwall also attracting attention as serious options – both also having shown a little more go-forward in their limited showings. This loss makes it three on the bounce for the new Wallabies coach. Two devastating losses to the All Blacks in October, and now a disappointing start to the Northern Hemisphere legs of the Nations Championship. With an often-dangerous Scotland up next at Scottish Gas Murrayfield Stadium, Kiss will need his men to bounce back and kick into gear if he’s to fend off the circling jackals. title: England player ratings v Australia: Henry Pollock-led Pom Squad returns in 'lethal fashion' amid 'big mister efforts' from the pack - Planet Rugby
content: Henry Pollock (left) and Maro Itoje (right) were among the key performers for England in their win over Australia Following England’s 45-22 win over Australia in the opening Test of November’s Nations Championship block, here is how we scored Steve Borthwick’s side. 15 George Furbank: A reminder of why he has remained at the top of the full-back depth chart despite a two-year wait for a Test cap. Supremely classy in attack, adding his typical playmaking skills into the mix and chucking a beautiful first-half assist and setting up the chance for Jack van Poortvliet’s score in the second-half. Very, very strong return to the side, as he stole the show in a big win. 9 14 Tommy Freeman: Once he got a foothold into the contest, he didn’t look back. Grew into the game wonderfully well to become an increasingly prominent cog in England’s attack, particularly in the second-half as he bagged two nice assists. 8 13 Henry Slade: His try-saving tackle in the second-half was his highlight moment, but it came after a lot of nice flashes across the game. Like Freeman, he never took a backwards step after getting into his groove, showing those deft handling skills in a free-flowing attack and kicking the absolute leather off the ball with his boot. Named Man of the Match too. 8 12 Seb Atkinson: Yet again showed why he is being given the reins at number 12 with some lovely work in tandem with Fin Smith, but was another back to withdraw through injury. 7 France suffer fly-half crisis ahead of Springboks showdown as injuries mount for Fabien Galthié 11 Immanuel Feyi-Waboso: The best player on the pitch whilst he was on, but his day was cut short through an ankle issue. He really hasn’t had it easy on the injury front of late, so hopefully this isn’t a lengthy layoff. 8 10 Fin Smith: Steered the ship really nicely in a big win, showing no signs that he was even remotely an injury headache earlier this week. Just seemed to get a real tune out of his backline, combining really nicely with those around him and having some gorgeous individual moments along the way. 8 9 Jack van Poortvliet: Could have easily gone south after that interception in the first-half, but he responded in the best way possible with a try of his own soon after. That came as a result of some nice work around the park, too, as he continues to cement his spot as England’s main number nine. 7 8 Ben Earl: The sort of performance we’ve come to expect from him in an England shirt. Things always seemed to happen whenever he touched the ball, often the first to really break down the stubborn Wallabies defence, and that helped set the platform for them to pull away late on. 8 7 Ben Curry: A very solid effort from the returning back-rower, who looked right at home back on the big stage. Just chucked himself into the battle up front to good effect, neutralising the Australian back-row in the process. Bodes well moving forward, after a lengthy layoff. 7 Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. 6 Ollie Chessum: Continues to look the part with six on his back. Gave England a really unique threat in attack when left as the wide forward, bagging a try in the process, but backed that up with some strong efforts in the ugly areas of the game. 8 5 Alex Coles: Nailed the nuts and bolts of a Test lock, as he always seems to do in the White jersey. Packed a real punch in defence, fared well in the lineout and simply ran his blood to water. 7 4 Maro Itoje (c): Big mister effort from the skipper, whose roar in the first-half reflected just how pumped up he was for this one. Led from the front in pretty much every aspect, posting a game-high 17 tackles in the process, and pleasingly looked for new and inventive ways to get his hand on the ball in attack too. Just lots to like, really. 8 The ‘unique’ reason Springboks stars are taking massive pay cuts to return from Japan 3 Joe Heyes: Solid stuff once more from the tighthead. Enjoyed a good old-fashioned ding-dong with Angus Bell in the scrum, with both giving as good as they got in that department, while he customarily got about in the loose to strong effect. 7 2 Jamie George: A real leaders’ effort from George, who helped lay the foundations in the tight. Once more fared well in the set-piece and got about in the loose, and was welcomed by a nice reception on his exit, which was certainly deserved. 7 1 Fin Baxter: Another returner from a long-term absence, and another who left his mark. Fared pretty well in the scrums, all told, and chucked himself about to good effect in defence too. Bodes well moving forward. 7 Replacements: The Pom Squad was back in all its glory today, and it was back in absolutely lethal fashion too. Henry Pollock lit the touchpaper for their efforts with a dazzling cameo in the backline, scoring two tries and causing all sorts of havoc along the way, while the rest of the unit followed upon their introductions to power through the Wallabies. This was a big part of their unbeaten run last November, and it looks to be a major tactic for Borthwick once more. 9 READ MORE: Eddie Jones: ‘That can be the difference between winning and losing’ Following confirmation of England's 23-man squad to take on the Wallabies, here's our take on the key winners and losers from the selection. title: Pre Game Injury Update - Lions v Dolphins - Yahoo Sports
content: Sunday has supplied one important answer for the Miami Dolphins. Unfortunately for their defense, it belongs to Detroit. Amon-Ra St. Brown is active despite the rib injury that left him questionable after a week of limited practices, according to the Lions' official game-day report. Miami must prepare for the receiver, not for the possibility that he might be missing. That is a meaningful distinction. St. Brown enters with 53 catches, 571 receiving yards and five touchdowns, the Lions report. His availability preserves an established option for Jared Goff. Miami cannot build its coverage plan around a Friday designation that Sunday has already resolved. Detroit also has Sione Vaki available after he was listed as questionable with an ankle injury. Jacob Saylors will not play because of his neck injury. The Lions elevated Jabari Small from the practice squad Saturday, giving their running-back group another option with Saylors inactive. Availability does not establish how those touches will be divided. Miami's running-back picture requires more caution. DolphinsTalk reported, citing NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, that Jaylen Wright is expected to miss the game with his quadriceps injury. That is stronger than Friday's questionable designation, but this draft does not have Miami's complete verified inactive list. title: Tromso v Bodo/Glimt: Fan injured after falling through hole in away stand - BBC
content: Tromso's Romssa Arena, pictured before a Conference League game against Brighton in August, is 200 miles inside the Arctic Circle A fan was taken to hospital after a number of Bodo/Glimt supporters fell through a hole in the away stand at Tromso. The Norwegian top-flight match at Romssa Arena on Sunday was paused just before half-time after Bodo keeper Nikita Haikin called for the referee's attention. Bodo/Glimt press officer Simen Pedersen told the Reuters news agency that "up to five people fell through the stands". "We stood and bounced to a supporter song, then the floor gave way," Bodo supporter Andrine Moen told local newspaper Verdens Gang, as reported by Reuters. "It cracked in two in the row in front of us. There were at least two people who fell through the floor, but we don't know how far they fell or how many fell in total." The remaining Bodo supporters were moved into other parts of the ground before the match resumed. The match at Tromso's stadium - the northernmost venue in Norway's Eliteserien - was played in heavy rain. The score was 0-0 at the time of the incident, but Bodo forward Ola Brynhildsen scored twice after the game resumed to give the league leaders a 2-0 win. Bodo are locked in a title battle with Viking and the Eliteserien season is set to finish in the first week of December. title: Liverpool Player Ratings v Crystal Palace: Alisson Becker Crucial To Reds Victory - Yahoo Sports
content: Liverpool returned to winning ways as they comfortably dispatched a low-confidence Crystal Palace side, winning 3-1 at Selhurst Park to go into the international break in the top four. Alexis Mac Allister opened the scoring with a header from a Szoboszlai free-kick, before Barcola and Wirtz combined early in the second half to double the Reds' lead. Then, as the home side continued to push for a goal, Alexander Isak finished off a flowing LFC counter-attack, ensuring that despite a late converted penalty for the Eagles, it would be the Merseyside outfit that left with all three points. Here are our player ratings (out of 10) following this away win. Heavily criticised in the last week or two, Alisson Becker showed everyone today why he is still one of the best in the world at what he does. Two crucial saves in the first half, to keep the score at 0-0, then another big save in the second half and he was unlucky to not leave Selhurst Park with a clean sheet. Offered very little going forward, with the opposition wing-back keeping the Hungarian pinned back, and defensively, he was shaky, to say the least, giving away a penalty late in the game. Up against a physical Strand Larsen for most of the game, he kept the striker quiet and made a few important blocks. A player who needed to right the wrongs from the Fenerbahce loss midweek was Jeremy Jacquet, and he certainly did that today. The defender looked back to his defensive best, making essential interceptions and stopping crosses from reaching their intended targets. Another strong display from the Barcelona loanee, Araujo returned to the starting XI after being rested in the Champions League and showed why he has become one of Iraola's most important players. Scored the goal to put the Reds in the lead after a few set pieces beforehand, where he looked like a real threat. Put in several good set-piece deliveries, but still gave away the ball far too much when on the counter-attack. A fairly anonymous game midweek, Barcola looked better this afternoon, capped off with a brilliant cross to get an assist for Wirtz's goal. Took his goal very well, a calm and composed finish to the keeper's right-hand side, and does a lot of the work on and off the ball that people rarely notice. While he didn't get on the scoresheet, his work rate, both offensively and defensively, was very good today. Had a chance very early in the game that, if the Swede had a better first touch, could have been a goal. Despite this, he looked sharp throughout the game, kept going, and eventually got the goal that his performance deserved. Came off the bench and added some real energy to the side, and was able to use that to exploit the space behind late in the game to help set up Liverpool's third. He was subbed on when the game needed control and composure, which is exactly what he provided. Had a few bright moments after coming on, but LFC mainly attacked down the opposite flank. The Welshman was only on for the last 10 minutes of the game. Like Koumas, he was brought on to see out the match, and while they conceded late on, there wasn't much he could do. The Brazilian shot-stopper has been linked with a move away from Anfield at the end of the season, with Iraola even coming out and explaining he wants him to stay but doesn't know if that will be the case. However this hasn't affected his performance today, as he was the main reason why Liverpool secured the win. Two huge saves in the first half, another in the second half, looking every bit like the goalkeeper Reds' fans have grown to love over the last eight years.

title: Breaking down the two controversial penalty incidents in Sunderland v Chelsea - The Independent
content: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in Enzo Le Fee scored the winner from the spot after Cole Palmer was denied at the other end Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. It was a tale of two penalties at the Stadium of Light as Sunderland defeated Chelsea to move off the bottom of the Premier League. First, Cole Palmer saw appeals waved away following a challenge from the side from Sunderland’s Luke O’Nien on the edge of the area. Then, at the other end, Sunderland striker Brian Brobbey won a penalty when he went down under the challenge of Chelsea’s Levi Colwill. Referee Jarred Gillett pointed to the spot and Enzo Le Fee converted to give Sunderland the lead and they held on to claim a vital victory. Palmer, who was left out of England’s squad by Thomas Tuchel on Friday, had performed some superb skill to make space and dribble towards the box. He got away from the challenge of Sunderland substitute Jules Ahoka, who had replaced injured captain Granit Xhaka, before O’Nien came in from the side. O’Nien’s left leg appears to come across Palmer, crashing into him and bringing him down without touching the ball, but referee Gillett waved play on. The incident was checked by VAR, however, with official Nick Hopton ruling that the contact between O’Nien and Palmer took place outside the area. Palmer’s momentum meant he went down in the box, but the Premier League Match Centre confirmed that “any contact with Palmer occurs outside the penalty area.” The Sunderland striker was a handful for the Chelsea centre-backs and Brobbey got a roll on Colwill to drive into the box. Both players had a hold of each other as Brobbey turned. The Dutchman had his left arm on Colwill’s back while Colwill had his right arm on Brobbey’s shirt. The contact continued as Brobbey entered the box, but what appeared to trip him up was when his right foot clipped his left and he tumbled to the ground. The Chelsea players around Colwill immediately appealed, but Gillett pointed to the spot. Colwill may have also clipped Brobbey’s heels, but it was unclear. Former Premier League referee Darren Cann told the BBC that Gillett was “spot on” to award the penalty, however. ”Brobbey and Levi Colwill were tussling outside the box and then it appeared there was lower leg contact on Brobbey which brought him down,” he said. “Gillett was in the perfect position to see the infringement and award the penalty.” Colwill was brought off at half-time, with Chelsea midfielder Moises Caicedo dropping into defence for Xabi Alonso’s side. But Chelsea still fell to a fourth defeat in eight Premier League games as they failed to seriously threaten Sunderland in the second half. The Black Cats had lost five of their previous six in the Premier League to fall to the bottom of the table, but claimed their first win in eight. It relieves the pressure on under-fire Regis Le Bris ahead of the upcoming international break. title: Would You Rather: Cadillac Escalade IQ vs. Escalade-V - Car and Driver
content: For about $160,000, are you taking the 682-hp supercharged gas Escalade or the 750-hp electric one? A lot of companies build EV models that have an internal-combustion analogue, with the guiding principle of, “the car you liked before, but electric.” There’s a tight thematic cohesiveness to that approach—a BMW i3 and M340i each endeavor to arrive at their optimized level of BMW 3-ness despite the differing powertrains—but the Cadillac Escalade is not like that. Yes, there are gas and electric versions, but they’re similar only inasmuch as they each avidly pursue the high-level Escalade goals of cosseting bigness and cocky braggadocio. When Tony Soprano got an Escalade in season 5 of The Sopranos, the only question around that casting decision was, what took so long? Today Tony would have more choices in his pursuit of the maximum expression of GM SUV, as do any of us with about $160,000 to spend. Namely, would you rather have a supercharged V-8 Escalade-V or an electric Escalade IQ? Cadillac designed the Escalade-V’s exhaust to be extra boisterous, adding a 360-degree loop to the passenger’s-side pipe to equalize the length with the driver’s-side counterpart, for maximum sonic awesomeness. The IQ does not have equal-length dual exhaust. Whatever exhaust it does produce will get you into a tedious and possibly confrontational discussion of well-to-wheel emissions with your uncle at Thanksgiving. However, you’ll never have to worry about thieves stealing your catalytic converters, so I’ll call that one a draw. Looking at the specs, I’m surprised to see that the Escalade-V weighs eight pounds more than the IQ. Hold on, that doesn’t sound right—let me check my notes—sorry, my curb-weight figure for the Escalade-V inadvertently included a Toyota GR86 parked on its roof. Remove that extra car, and the supercharged Escalade is quite a bit lighter: 6290 pounds for the V, and a pavement-crushing 9120 pounds for the IQ. Despite the weight disparity, the two Slades are evenly matched in a drag race, with the 750-hp IQ trailing the 682-hp V by a couple tenths of a second to 60 mph (4.5 seconds to 4.3). On a rolling start from 5 mph, they’re tied at 4.7 seconds, and passing a dawdler will be a quicker task in the IQ: 50 to 70 mph in 2.6 seconds, versus 3.1 seconds for the loud Caddy. Now, I’m old enough to remember the days when a Ferrari 458 Italia felt like it had pretty decent passing power, but the Escalade IQ’s 2.1-second 30-to-50-mph time beats the Ferrari by a tenth. If the IQ had been part of our Chariots of the Gods comparison test in 2011, its 50-to-70-mph time would have slotted it a tenth of a second behind the 458 and two-tenths ahead of the McLaren MP4-12C. Neither of those, when accelerating, heave their hoods skyward like a 70-foot Viking sportfish climbing on a plane, but the Escalade IQ certainly does. And they say EVs don’t bring any drama to the experience—behind the wheel, the IQ accelerating like my favorite Ferrari of all time feels as improbable as it actually is, like the vehicle itself is struggling to cope with its superpowers. An Escalade-V drives more like a mutant CT5-V Blackwing, and it’s definitely the Escalade where the driver’s seat is more desirable than one of the chauffeur chairs in back. If we accept that one of the primary goals for an Escalade is to project brash confidence, and that hugeness is fundamental to that project, the Escalade IQ wins going away. It reminds me of a scaled-up Rolls-Royce Cullinan in the side profile, and there’s a lot of side to behold: the IQ is more than a foot longer than the gas-powered Escalade. It’s also just newer, and I think it helps the premium aura not to have a bunch of Chevys and GMCs out there copping your style with very similar bodies. Also: rear-axle steering is unequivocally a flex, and the internal-combustion Escalade doesn’t have it. Inside, both Escalades offer huge screens, lots of leather, and power-operated doors. However, only the IQ is eligible for the Curated by Cadillac program, wherein buyers fork over an additional $54,995 and get to choose from a huge palette of colors, inside and out. With 44 interior color choices, you can certainly spec a one-of-one IQ, while the Escalade-V sticks with “Yukon Denali, but fancier” as a guiding principle. Advantage, IQ. When we’re discussing EVs versus internal combustion, range is usually an easy win for the gas-powered candidate. But not here—the Escalade-V has an EPA-rated 312 miles of range, while the IQ gets a 465-mile rating. Yes, the V will refuel a lot quicker, but you’ll be stopping way more often. And if your gas pump stops at $100, you might technically need to fill twice to top off the 24-gallon tank with premium. Another factor I have to consider is rap music references, and on that front the Escalade-V is the easy winner, if only because the IQ is too new—most Escalade lyrics concern gas-powered models by default. Cadillac did hire Big Boi from Outkast to rap about the IQ, but that doesn’t count. (“Escalade IQ, this is the intro to, the all-electric Cadillac perfection ...”) I’m sure we’ll get there eventually: “Rolling in the IQ to the house with a view, IQ got the roof see-through, park the IQ next to the other ’cause I just bought two.” Finally, I think part of the Escalade mystique has always hinged on leadership. This is a boss truck, from Sopranos to Succession. And where are the luxury winds blowing? It seems to me that in this space, which is to say “not a V-12 Ferrari,” the market is amenable to electrification and the technology is progressing fast. GM just announced that its forthcoming battery chemistry will improve range while being 20 percent more compact. There will come a time, maybe not far off, when EVs just make more sense objectively (they already do, depending on use case) and internal combustion will be the nostalgia play. So in this Would You Rather, I’m embracing that future and going for the Escalade IQ. The V is charming, but for $160,000, the IQ better fulfills the role of flagship SUV—quick, cocky, luxurious, and incontrovertibly baller. Ezra Dyer is a Car and Driver senior editor and columnist. He's now based in North Carolina but still remembers how to turn right. He owns a 2009 GEM e4 and once drove 206 mph. Those facts are mutually exclusive. title: PREVIEW | Atlético Madrid v FC Barcelona - Official FC Barcelona Website
content: FC Barcelona's season got off to a record-breakingly brilliant start, with nine straight league victories, all by two or more goals. Which makes it all the more extraordinary to think that, should they lose this Sunday's 9pm CET kick-off at the Metropolitano, it will be Atlético Madrid who go into the next international break as league leaders. It's Barça's job to make sure that doesn't happen on one of the toughest away trips in European football. Victory would put five points between themselves and Atlético, who currently trail Hansi Flick's side by just two points, and would also keep Real Madrid at bay, who won 3-0 at Valencia in Saturday night to draw level with Barça on 30 points. The blaugrana come into the game in buoyant mood after a 6-1 win over Alavés in La Liga and Tuesday's 3-0 Champions League victory against Aston Villa. Diego Simeone's side have been in tremendous domestic form, winning their last seven league matches, including a 2-1 victory over Real Madrid. With nine wins, one draw and one defeat from 11 games, Atlético have the best defensive record in La Liga, having conceded just eight times. Their Champions League campaign has been less convincing, however, and they go into Sunday's game following a 2-0 home defeat to Bayern Munich. With Julián Álvarez, Alexander Sørloth and Ademola Lookman among their attacking options, Atlético pose a formidable challenge. But Barça have scored a remarkable 46 goals in just 11 league games, a tally surpassed at this stage of a Spanish league season only by Athletic Club in 1930/31, with 49. There is unfinished business between these sides after Atlético eliminated Barça from both the Copa del Rey and the Champions League last season. The blaugrana did win 2-1 at the Metropolitano in the second leg of their European quarter-final, but it was Atlético who progressed 3-2 on aggregate. The recent league record in Madrid, however, favours Barça. They have won on each of their last four league visits to Atlético and could become only the third team to record five consecutive away league victories against the colchoneros. And the teams will not have to wait long for their next meeting. Atlético visit Spotify Camp Nou on Wednesday 2 December for a league fixture brought forward because of the Spanish Super Cup. Barça remain without Dani Olmo, Roony Bardghji and Xavi Espart through injury, while Rodrigo Hernández is also unavailable after being forced off against Aston Villa. There is better news concerning Eric Garcia and Andreas Christensen, with Hansi Flick confirming that both will be with the squad for Sunday's game. Atlético, meanwhile, are without the injured Cristian Romero and Johnny Cardoso. Hansi Flick is fully aware of the importance of Sunday's meeting between the top two, but insists that the title race is a long one. "We know they're a fantastic team with a great coach, but we'll give everything to win tomorrow. There's still a long way to go in the league." The German coach is also refusing to dwell on last season's cup eliminations at Atlético's hands. "The past isn't relevant. We know they're very good, but we want to win and we have to win. We want to be leaders going into the break, and that's why we've worked hard."

title: All Blacks player ratings v Scotland: Beauden Barrett's 'renaissance' continues while scrum shines in fine all-round display - Planet Rugby
content: Josh Moorby, Beauden Barrett and Ethan De Groot all impressed for the All Blacks against Scotland. After their 43-21 victory over Scotland in their Nations Championship clash at Murrayfield, here’s how the All Blacks team performed on Saturday. 15 Beauden Barrett: The veteran All Blacks utility back has revived his Test career recently, and his renaissance continued in this match as he kept Scotland’s defenders on their toes throughout. Barrett‘s attacking efforts were rewarded with two tries, which brought up a half-century of five-pointers for the All Blacks at Test level and he was solid under the high ball. 8 14 Will Jordan: Although New Zealand’s try-scoring machine did not cross the whitewash in this clash, he asked plenty of questions of Scotland‘s defence and finished with a team-high 59 metres gained. 7 13 Quinn Tupaea: The Chiefs midfielder impressed with his distribution skills in the outside channels but made his biggest contribution on defence where he made 12 tackles and won a crucial turnover. 8 12 Jordie Barrett: The youngest of the Barrett brothers has been in fine form throughout 2026 and this clash was no different as he put in a superb all-round performance. Was brilliant on either side of the ball before being forced off after 65 minutes following a head clash with Blair Kinghorn. 8 11 Josh Moorby: The Hurricanes flyer looked dangerous with ball in hand and crossed for a try early in the second half while he also did well in the aerial duels. 7 10 Damian McKenzie: The diminutive playmaker was shifted to fly-half from full-back with great success against the Wallabies and that continued against Scotland where his playmaking skills created several try-scoring opportunities for his team-mates. Missed some shots at goal off the kicking tee, though. 7 9 Cam Roigard: Continued with his outstanding form as he provided a slick service to his outside backs while also proving to be an attacking threat around the fringes. Replaced by Cortez Ratima on the hour-mark. 7 Scotland v New Zealand: Five takeaways as All Blacks pass litmus test with ‘flying colours’ despite benefitting from ‘clear and obvious’ obsession 8 Wallace Sititi: The 24-year-old was in the thick of the action from the outset and was rewarded with a well-taken try after four minutes and continued to shine on attack as the match progressed. Also spent some time in the sin bin for straying offside on defence late in the second half, but Sititi can be happy with his efforts as he finished with 50 metres gained. 7 7 Peter Lakai: Like his back-row partner Sititi, Lakai was also yellow-carded for a cynical defensive indiscretion after 23 minutes but apart from that, he got through plenty of work on either side of the ball and also crossed the whitewash. 7 6 Tupou Vaa’i: Was on the field for 71 minutes before being replaced by Christian Lio-Willie but Vaa’i proved a handy option at the back of the lineout during his time on the field. Also got through plenty of work on defence where he made 16 hits. 7 5 Fabian Holland: The All Blacks’ Dutch-born enforcer did what was expected of him at the coalface of their forward effort as he won his fair share of lineout balls and was superb on defence where he made 17 tackles. 7 4 Scott Barrett: Although the former All Blacks skipper was anonymous on attack, he made up for that with a huge defensive effort as he finished with a team-high 21 tackle execution and he also won a couple of turnovers. 8 3 Fletcher Newell: The All Blacks held the upper hand at scrum time as they won some penalties at the set-piece and Newell will be happy with his efforts in that department as he won his direct duel against Rory Sutherland. Eventually replaced by Pasilio Tosi after 63 minutes. 8 2 Codie Taylor (c): Another solid performance from the experienced hooker who impressed as a ball carrier, where he was rewarded with a five-pointer for his efforts, while also shining on defence where he made 14 tackles. Replaced by Asafo Aumua in the 56th minute. 7 1 Ethan de Groot: Like Newell, the burly loosehead prop will be delighted with his scrummaging efforts as he was excellent in the set-piece but also impressed at close quarters on attack and scored a deserved try early in the second half. George Bower replaced him after 50 minutes. 8 Replacements: This match was in the balance at half-time with the All Blacks holding a slender 24-21 lead but their head coach Dave Rennie used his replacements intelligently after the interval. Bower, Tosi and Aumua continued with the excellent scrummaging when coming on in the second half and the latter added the final nail in Scotland’s coffin when he scored New Zealand’s seventh try in the 68th minute. 8 READ MORE: Ex-All Blacks forward makes Hurricanes return as Super Rugby champions confirm new coaching hires Beauden Barrett has proven his critics wrong since returning to the All Blacks side, leaving Dave Rennie impressed. It wasn't long ago that Beauden Barrett's Rugby World Cup hopes were in doubt. Mike Blair has revealed how important the experienced playmaking duo Beauden Barrett and Damian McKenzie are to the All Blacks' cause on attack. Beauden Barrett has struggled for most of 2026 but a positional switch has certainly helped the All Blacks legend. © Planet Sport Limited 2026 • All Rights Reserved

title: Cray Wanderers v Stockport County: Cray set for maiden FA Cup first-round appearance - BBC
content: Cray Wanderers, one of the four oldest clubs in England, are playing in their 78th FA Cup campaign this season If at first you do not succeed, try and try again. And again. Until, at the 78th attempt, you finally make it. Formed in 1860, Cray Wanderers are one of the oldest football clubs in the world - and the oldest club in London still in existence. And yet the Wands had never reached the FA Cup first round in their 166-year history. It was perhaps fitting that Cray only just scraped through in the fourth qualifying round against Bedford Town in dramatic fashion to achieve something they have tried and failed to do 77 times before. Following a 0-0 draw on 17 October away at Bedford, it was back to Flamingo Park for a replay three days later. The game ended 1-1 after 90 minutes and went to extra time. Bedford then took the lead in the 101st minute, only for Cray striker Ade Yusuff - who has scored in all four rounds so far - to make it 2-2 and force a penalty shootout. Wands goalkeeper JJ Briggs, who is on loan from Cambridge United, made two saves in the shootout to help pave the way for history to be made in Chislehurst. When teenager Jakob Lowe stuck away his effort from 12 yards to seal a 4-3 win on penalties, the scale of the moment was not lost on club captain Frankie Raymond. Cray Wanderers midfielder and captain Frankie Raymond, right, says qualifying for the FA Cup first round is a "great occasion" for the club "It means a massive amount to us all," Raymond told BBC London. "It's a club steeped in history and to be the first set of players and staff to take the club to the first round is a massive achievement for everyone." Raymond is right about the remarkable history at Cray. From helping to form the Kent League in 1894 and serving as a nursery club to Woolwich Arsenal - known today simply as Arsenal - between 1895 and 1907, much has gone before in this little pocket of south-east London. And in more recent times, the Cray Wanderers youth setup is where it all started for Manchester City and England centre-back Marc Guehi at the age of six. BBC to show Cray Wanderers v Stockport & Altrincham v Notts County Cray are 18th in the Isthmian League Premier Division - the seventh tier of the English football pyramid. Tim O'Shea's side are only outside the relegation zone on goal difference, although they do have at least four games in hand on the teams around them. The journey to the FA Cup first round has been far from simple for the Wands, with three replays required in the four qualifying rounds, meaning they have played seven matches - with 660 minutes of football - to make their dream a reality. And their reward for getting this far? One of the hardest draws possible at this stage of the competition. They will host League One's second-placed team Stockport County, live on BBC Two on Sunday (14:15 GMT). FA Cup first round: Cray Wanderers v Stockport County Ex-Hornchurch and Folkestone Invicta striker Ade Yusuff has scored 11 goals in all competitions for Cray Wanderers so far this season For Cray's top goalscorer Yusuff, Friday will be spent in the school classroom where he works as a teacher before his attentions turn to the biggest game in the club's history at the weekend. The school corridors have been full of "really excited" pupils chatting about the upcoming encounter against the Hatters, the 32-year-old said. "They're really looking forward to it, they're really proud," Yusuff added. Despite Stockport being 112 league positions higher than Cray, Yusuff hopes he can keep his cup goalscoring run going. "I don't see why not," he said. "The team are in really good form and when the boys are creating chances the way they are, I always back myself - no matter who it's against - to score." Yusuff also believes they can cause an upset, having already knocked out National League South side Maidstone United and National League North team Bedford. "I think it's all about momentum," he said. "We've beaten higher teams in different positions in the earlier rounds. I think it's about believing in ourselves. "A lot of the boys here have really good careers ahead of them. They have to have these occasions and these moments so they can say: 'I can do it and I can achieve something myself'." Mark Hunt has been following Cray Wanderers since 2010 Someone else who refuses to rule out a giant-killing is Cray Wanderers fan Mark Hunt. "Anything could happen," he said. "There's always a David and Goliath story. We had one last year when Macclesfield beat Crystal Palace. "There's a big, big gap between Macclesfield and Palace. Why can't it be Stockport v Cray? "Most people expect the underdogs to fail, most times they will, but a few slip through the net. "You get one shot at it. And the fact it goes straight to a penalty shootout, no replay, no VAR, artificial pitch - it could go in our favour." Attendances at Flamingo Park fluctuate between 130 and 900, but Sunday's tie with Stockport sold out in five minutes, with 2,500 fans expected. "It means the world," added Hunt. "It's been such a long time coming. It's something we've been waiting for for so long, just to get a shot at a Stockport County. title: RAF Abu Dhabi: Khamzat Chimaev v Colby Covington and all you need to know - The National
content: Real American Freestyle (RAF) makes its Middle East debut this month in Abu Dhabi. RAF is the first unscripted professional freestyle wrestling league, bringing Olympic champions, world medalists, NCAA standouts, and top MMA crossover athletes together in a modern fight-night format. RAF Abu Dhabi: What are the rules of freestyle wrestling? The inaugural RAF Abu Dhabi event marks the start of a five-year partnership between Real American Freestyle, the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi (DCT Abu Dhabi), and the UAE Wrestling Federation. It follows RAF’s international events in Tbilisi, Georgia and Moscow. RAF Abu Dhabi takes place on Saturday, November 14. The event will take place at the Etihad Arena on Yas Island. The UAE star will face former UFC welterweight contender Colby Covington for the American's Cruiserweight Crossover Championship. Chimaev, an elite grappler and former UFC middleweight champion, is undefeated in freestyle wrestling and will be looking to make it 28 straight wins when he takes on the American. He has fought on three RAF cards this year, starting with a 44-second pinfall over Dillon Danis at RAF 10 in June. A mass melee broke out after the referee's whistle involving members of both teams. Covington has warned there could be similar scenes on the mats in Abu Dhabi. Chimaev's rivalry with Covington dates back to when both were in the UFC, although an MMA matchup never materialised, and has escalated significantly ahead of their upcoming match in Abu Dhabi. Covington, who retired from MMA in May, has repeatedly criticised Chimaev, calling him someone who has “had everything handed to him”. “I think I would break Khamzat. He doesn't have the cardio to keep up with me,” Covington said. “I will bring those quitter tendencies out of him.” Chimaev has dismissed Covington as an “easy fight” and said he can “break his neck, finally”. The UAE athlete said Covington will “need an ambulance” to send him home after the American complained about having to defend his title outside the US. RAF Abu Dhabi features a stacked card headlined by Chimaev-Covington. Arman Tsarukyan will face Neiman Gracie in a catchweight crossover match. Tsarukyan, the No 1-ranked contender in the UFC's lightweight division, boasts an 11-2 record in the world's leading MMA organisation. The Armenian heads to the UAE capital with an 8-1 RAF record, including six wins by technical fall. He faces Brazilian Gracie, a three-time World BJJ bronze medallist. Former UFC bantamweight title contender Umar Nurmagomedov was also added to the card. The Dagestani will take on Uriah Faber, who returns for his third RAF match. Faber is a former MMA champion and the founder of Team Alpha Male. American Kyle Dake will defend his cruiserweight championship against Turkmenistan’s Alp Arslan Begenjov, while Kennedy Blades puts her women’s middleweight title on the line against fellow American Bella Mir, daughter of former UFC heavyweight champion Frank Mir. Russia’s Zabit Magomedsharipov takes on Giga Chikadze of Georgia in a welterweight crossover bout, while Team USA Olympic gold medallist Jordan Burroughs meets Belarusian Azamat Nurykau at middleweight. Also joining the card is reigning RAF light heavyweight champion Kyle Snyder, who will face Shamil Erdogan. A quartet of Arab athletes will make their RAF debuts at Etihad Arena: Bahrain’s Hamza Kooheji and Murtaza Talha, Jordan’s Ali Al Qaisi, and Egypt’s Osama Elsaidy are all set to compete. Tickets can be purchased at www.etihadarena.ae and ticketmaster.ae. Ticket prices start from Dh95.
