title: France v Fiji: Five takeaways as 'exquisite' Antoine Dupont stars but injury to key man creates 'crisis' ahead of Springboks showdown - Planet Rugby
content: Theo Attissogbe heading over for a try for France against Fiji. France ran in eight tries to beat Fiji 54-17 in Lyon, with Antoine Dupont exquisite at the base and Geoffrey Doumayrou’s new defence impressive, but the loss of key man Romain Ntamack leaves Fabien Galthié with a fly-half crisis of endemic proportions six days before the Springboks rumble into Paris. Nobody does a rugby opening ceremony quite like France, and with a stunning new Adidas kit, a sold-out Groupama Stadium and Dupont and Ntamack together in la charnière for the first time since March 2025, this had all the expectation and makings of a special night. Galthié had promised something spectacular, and for long stretches we got it: eight tries, a player of the match performance from Dupont that was as good as anything we’ve seen from him in a blue shirt in years, and an attacking sequence early in the second half, ignited by the Toulouse nine, that was like somebody flicking a light switch on. But it was also a match and a French side that, at times, delivered a lot less than it promised. It took the hosts 14 minutes to score, after a start that saw Ntamack’s kick-off go straight into touch, Théo Attissogbé fumble the first contestable and the first French lineout throw go in crooked, and even with the game won they kept shooting themselves in the foot at the set-piece, dropping four driving mauls in the second half and effectively crippling the same weapon that had earned them a penalty try in the first. Then there’s the injury list, which now includes Ntamack, off after 33 minutes with a suspected left shoulder subluxation. It was, in the final analysis, l’œuf du curé: very good in parts, bad in others, and the parts that weren’t will worry Galthié far more than the scoreline suggests. Fiji, for their part, looked transformed in structure and organisation since the summer’s 73-8 humbling at the hands of England. Jake White said before kick-off that he wanted defence, discipline and territory from his side, and he got one of the three; the other two will need work before Dublin. Dupont was exquisite tonight. With Ntamack gone and Maxime Lucu, a scrum-half by trade, moving to 10, France needed someone to run the game, and Dupont simply took it on himself, roaming across the field looking for space, throwing 75 passes, beating five defenders and having a hand in try after try: the cross-kick that started Jean-Baptiste Gros’s opener, the opening that sent Sipili Falatea back against the grain, a long left-handed pass to put Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang away, a lightning break and flip pass behind him for Yoram Moefana that covered 60 metres in a flash, and finally a try of his own off the back of a driving maul with two minutes left. He also won the ball back on the touchline for Attissogbé’s try. 18 months ago he was recovering from a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament, but tonight he looked like a man who’d never been away. World Rugby rankings: How Saturday’s Nations Championship and Nations Cup action affects the standings Outside Dupont, Moefana was something else, direct and powerful on both sides of the ball with 14 carries for 91 metres and six defenders beaten, whilst Grandidier-Nkanang is seriously quick and made 123 metres, the most on the pitch, with Attissogbé close behind on 112. Most importantly for France, their starting front-row was very, very good indeed. Gros made ten tackles without a miss, scored a try and smashed Fiji for a scrum penalty early in the second half, and Falatea is as good with ball in hand as any tighthead in the game, although his scrummaging only just held on, and next weekend he’ll have a much sterner task. Louis Bielle-Biarrey’s work rate was phenomenal despite Fiji shutting him down for an hour, and when he finally broke them open he set up Attissogbé’s try; he also spent time at first receiver for set-piece attack, as he does for UBB when Lucu plays at 10. François Cros made 14 tackles and was generally outstanding, but for one lapse, when Vinaya Habosi stepped him magnificently and left Cros grasping at thin air with nobody covering the backfield; miss one like that against South Africa and you are toast. Yet France’s back-row looked a tad unbalanced. Cros is a collision forward who does his best work alongside the ball-carrier rather than over the ball himself, and at eight he perhaps looked a little constrained; with Cameron Woki and Paul Boudehent on the flanks, France had no real jackal threat, nobody whose first instinct is to get his hands on the ball at the tackle, and as a result Fiji counter-rucked superbly, retaining 82 of their 83 rucks and winning seven turnovers to France’s three, with Kitione Salawa claiming his second straight after the break. The veteran Charles Ollivon came on for Florian Verhaeghe on 57 minutes to the biggest cheer of the night, and it’s pretty much a rugby fact that he is to Galthie’s France what Jamie Tartt is to Ted Lasso’s AFC Richmond,; a goal-hanging pest of the highest order. Within a minute he’d ripped the ball from a Fijian on the floor for Kalvin Gourgues’s try; by the 72nd he’d scored one himself, an absolute poacher’s finish from close range for his 20th Test try, a record for a French forward, and to cap his night he caught the lineout that launched Dupont’s final score. White will be happy with Fiji in some respects. Their press and shape were miles better than in July, their counter-rucking was outstanding, with Tevita Ikanivere leading from the front with 17 tackles, the most on the pitch, and Nathan Hughes, who beat seven defenders, produced his trademark pick-and-go straight through a ruck. Crucially, Fiji elected to keep the ball on the park; with France’s maul already producing a penalty try and a yellow card for Mesake Vocevoce, every kick to touch was an invitation to drive, so Fiji kicked long and infield instead, out-kicking France by 685 metres to 501 and holding them to 53-47 in territory. Opinion: Average All Blacks blunder on and why someone other than the Springboks will expose them The downside is that they barely attacked until the final quarter, carrying just 47 times all night, and the other two of White’s targets fell well short. Both of France’s first-half tries from close range came from Fijian penalties, and 29 missed tackles at 69 per cent is far too many against anyone, let alone Ireland next week. The late flourish was encouraging, with Habosi and Selestino Ravutaumada, after lovely interplay with Frank Lomani, matching France try for try over the last quarter of an hour, and it’s a sign of what this group can achieve once the structure White is building is in place. There’s a lesson in the numbers too: Fiji won the kicking metres, the ruck count and the turnover battle yet still lost by 37, which tells you how ruthlessly France turned possession into points in the red zone when they bothered to be accurate. One odd call deserves explaining, because it decided a try outcome and it left Fiji felt pretty aggrieved. A player can claim a mark only in his own 22, catching the ball cleanly direct from an opponent’s kick and calling “mark” as he does so, but the catch has to be completed, with the ball fully under control. When Dupont’s long pass sent Grandidier-Nkanang away and he kicked ahead, Vilimoni Botitu took the ball and called for the mark, but it came out as he hit the ground. A ball that comes loose on contact with the ground was never controlled, and no control means no mark, so the ball was live and Grandidier-Nkanang, following up his own kick, picked up and scored. Karl Dickson saw it, explained it clearly and got it absolutely spot on. France have had a greater turnover at fly-half this year than most modern governments manage in 10, and the injury list is now endemic. With Ntamack off, Matthieu Jalibert and Thomas Ramos already out and Antoine Hastoy injuring his ankle before the camp began, Galthié simply doesn’t have a specialist 10 of real calibre to call on, and it’s almost certain Maxime Lucu and Dupont will form la charnière against South Africa, with the uncapped Louis Le Brun, the only other option at 10 left in the squad. Lucu does bring a genuinely deep kicking game, but as a 10 he’s lateral and doesn’t drive a side forward, and against the Springboks’ line speed that will be a real concern. It’s ironic that the old Hospital-Dieu on the banks of the Rhône is now a beautiful hotel, because on tonight’s evidence Lyon might have needed to reopen it had France picked up any more injuries. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Galthié also needs his maul back, because four dropped drives in a half is one thing against Fiji, but against the Springboks it would be fatal. He needs to rebalance that back-row too; whilst Cros was good, Woki had his moments and Boudehent was very physical, Ollivon certainly made the case for his inclusion in his 23 minutes on the pitch, and it might need a rethink of the back five if France are to beat South Africa. Meanwhile, somewhere in Paris, the Springbok squad will be quietly munching biltong, drinking Klippies, FaceTiming their kids, sending each other Instagram messages and half-watching the video of this match, and take it from us, they’ll be worried about absolutely nothing whatsoever. title: Crystal Palace v Liverpool: Team news - Liverpool FC
content: Andoni Iraola reported no fresh injury concerns ahead of Crystal Palace v Liverpool, though Ryan Gravenberch is a doubt for the trip to Selhurst Park. Midfielder Gravenberch did not travel for Wednesday’s game at Fenerbahce due to the heel problem that also prevented him from playing against Arsenal last weekend. Reds head coach Iraola held his pre-Palace press conference on Friday afternoon and, when asked for a squad fitness update, replied: “The only doubt we will have is Ryan. The others will be the same as we have been. “The Ryan Gravenberch thing is a day-to-day thing, it’s a matter of pain. Let’s see if he can deal with the pain and he can help us.” Sunday’s 2pm GMT kick-off comes too soon for Jeremie Frimpong – who has missed the last five games because of a muscle issue – while Conor Bradley, Hugo Ekitike and Giovanni Leoni are long-term absentees. Bradley Barcola started as Liverpool’s central forward in the midweek Champions League defeat in Istanbul and Iraola was quizzed on the likelihood of the France international being deployed there again this season. “Bradley is a winger. He mostly has played as a left winger, sometimes as a right winger but also has played in PSG as a striker. It’s something that I wanted to try,” the boss said. “I thought against the centre-backs he could be a threat, especially in behind. But he’s a winger and he will be mostly, 90 per cent of the time, used as a winger. But I think it’s alternatives that I sometimes want to try. “I tried with Cody [Gakpo] against Chelsea, I think, in the Carabao Cup and not maybe from the beginning but it’s true that during the games I think it’s options that we can use when Alex [Isak] is tired and we need another type of striker. “We can use other strikers that we have but also wingers that can do a job there.” Andoni Iraola's pre-Crystal Palace press conference Palace, meanwhile, will be without forwards Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr on Sunday. Mateta is suspended after he was sent off in the Eagles’ loss to Tottenham Hotspur last weekend, while Sarr has not featured in their four most recent matches and will not return until after the November international break, according to manager Pierre Sage. Sage sees Eddie Nketiah and Jorgen Strand Larsen as options to replace Mateta, saying: “As you know, JP [Mateta] was injured at the beginning of the season. “There was the opportunity for Jorgen Strand Larsen and Eddie Nketiah to play. He will miss [the game], but we have to deal with it. We have big confidence in the other players. They’ve shown they are able to play and they are able to compete. “We need them in the play, we need them to press, we need them to score, to finalise the offensive play. Jorgen showed that against Ipswich and against Lech Poznan, that’s why we know he’s able to score. “Eddie scored against Fulham, he scored against Lech Poznan too, and Eddie is able to play as a No. 10 too. “That’s why we will see what will happen on Sunday – but we have some solutions.” Strand Larsen was an unused substitute for Palace’s 1-1 draw with Hoffenheim in the Europa League on Thursday night, following a three-match absence. Sage completed his pre-Liverpool media duties immediately after that game and, on Strand Larsen’s fitness, stated: “He didn’t play today because the scenario of the game was not positive for him to have the possibility to let him play. “But I think he’s able to play 60, 75 [minutes] and with the head and the stamina, maybe he can push this.” 'Now we have to react' - more from Iraola's pre-Palace press conference Crystal Palace 1-1 Hoffenheim (November 5): Henderson, Richards, Canvot, Ahanor, Khalaili, Timber, Wharton, Mitchell, Kamada, Pino, Mateta. Fenerbahce 3-2 Liverpool (November 4): Alisson, Gomez, Jacquet, Van Dijk, Tsimikas, Mac Allister, Nyoni, Munoz, Szoboszlai, Ngumoha, Barcola.

In touch at half-time down 21-24 after two All Blacks sin-binnings, Scotland couldn’t add to their score; frustrated by a string of penalties, they conceded 13 to eight and were unable to penetrate a dogged All Blacks defence. A key turnover by centre Quinn Tupaea, a constant threat in the midfield, regained momentum midway through the second half, when the game was meandering, to extend the All Blacks’ lead. Fullback Beauden Barrett benefited from the All Blacks’ attacking approach with two tries, including his 50th in Tests, but the pack's power took the sting out of Scotland. Lock Fabian Holland dominated the lineouts, supported by flanker Tupou Vaa’i, while the front row were controlled and consistent. That was evident when the first scrum of the game came in the 33rd minute, as the All Blacks, with only seven in the scrum, relieved pressure on their line. Then six minutes into the second half, off their own feed, their power earned a penalty out from Scotland’s line. While they didn’t score on the first chance, another Scottish infringement, this time in front of the posts, allowed halfback Cam Roigard to throw a long pass to second five-eighths Jordie Barrett, who threw another long ball to the unmarked left wing Josh Moorby, who scored. Three minutes later, after 51 minutes, Scotland captain Sione Tuipulotu was yellow-carded. The All Blacks took immediate toll, kicking for a lineout and winning the ball with Tupaea playing as stand-off to feed first five-eighths Damian McKenzie, who linked with Beauden Barrett to join the line for his second try of the game, his 50th, to take a 36-21 lead. Barrett pulled off a big defensive play in the 56th minute to break an 18-phase Scotland build-up and deny wing Kyle Steyn a potential try. The play lost momentum, but once Tupaea pulled off a superb tackle and won a turnover penalty, the All Blacks used their lineout to regain it. Vaa’i took the ball deep in the line and fed Lakai on the blindside, where replacement hooker Asafo Aumua ran unchallenged to score. Seven tries told the story of the action-packed first half, four of them to the All Blacks. Flanker Wallace Sititi scored after three minutes from a clever dummy lineout move, and prop Ethan de Groot (15 minutes) crossed off a tap penalty by halfback Cam Roigard just out from the line. That was followed by captain and hooker Codie Taylor (19 mins) crossing from a lineout drive. They lost Lakai to the sin-bin after the All Blacks conceded five consecutive penalties. But the All Blacks countered after a lineout penalty gave McKenzie the chance to throw a long pass to Beauden Barrett (30 mins), who raced into a gap to score. Scotland utilised their lineout drive for hooker Ewan Ashman to score two of his hat-trick of tries (seven and 37 minutes). He was required to run a little further for his third after Scotland ran the ball to the midfield where he made use of a gap created after Sititi’s 32nd minute yellow card. Scotland took the All Blacks on with their backlines, several times creating openings and forcing defensive penalties, while Moorby denied them a try by getting his hands under the ball in a goal-line tackle. The Scots were forced to make 143 tackles compared to 132, while they were unable to make the most of a breakdown advantage of 109-86. The All Blacks denied Scots dangerman first five-eighths Finn Russell to have an influence and that told in the final outcome. Scotland 21 ( Ewan Ashman 3 tries; Finn Russell 3 con) New Zealand 43 (Wallace Sititi, Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor, Beauden Barrett 2, Josh Moorby, Asafo Aumua tries;  Damian McKenzie 4 con). HT: 21-24

title: Arsenal 1-0 Hull City: How the players rated - BBC
content: Odegaard hits winner as Arsenal beat Hull to extend lead at top Arsenal needed a late goal from Martin Odegaard to beat a stubborn Hull side at Emirates Stadium. The Gunners, who thought they should have been awarded a penalty in the first half, looked like they would be frustrated by the Tigers before Odegaard followed up Noni Madueke's shot to tap in the winner. Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below. David Raya: A good save when Elliot Stroud drilled a low cross into the area. 6 Jurrien Timber: Not his best game in an Arsenal shirt. 5 Ezri Konsa: Another good performance, which is what is expected from him since signing for the Gunners. 7 Gabriel Magalhaes: Caught on the ball once in the middle of the pitch but the usual solid performance apart from that. 7 Riccardo Calafiori: A good defensive performance but not his usual impact when going forward. 6 Declan Rice: Went closest for Arsenal in the first half with an effort from the edge of the box but subbed as Arsenal chased a goal. 6 Bruno Guimaraes: The midfielder still seems to be getting up to the pace of the season. 6 Martin Odegaard: Scored the crucial goal for Arsenal. Injected pace into the Arsenal play whenever he got on the ball and deserved to score the winner. 8 Christos Tzolis: Lots of energy but not much quality from the winger. 5 Noni Madueke: A dangerous ball in followed by a driving run early in the game. Alongside Odegaard the winger was Arsenal's main threat and his shot resulted in the winner. 7 Kai Havertz: Disappointing first half and turned back instead of shooting when played through. Went down after a shirt pull for a penalty but was given offside after a VAR check. A poor performance. 4 Gyokeres (on 63, Havertz): Did not make much of an impact. 5 Merino (on 63, Rice): A calming influence when he came on. 6 Eze (on 69, Tzolis): Added some flair to the Arsenal attack. 6 Hincapie (on 69, Calafiori): A more traditional left back and overlapped as Arsenal pushed for the win. 6 Subs not used: Arrizabalaga, White, Mosquera, Lewis-Skelly. Konstantinos Tzolakis: Pushed Madueke's shot back into a dangerous area which resulted in the goal. 7 Lewie Coyle: A solid performance but replaced on the hour mark as Arsenal piled on the pressure. 6 Semi Ajayi: The centre-back seemed to be in the way of a lot of what came into the Hull penalty area. Came off with an injury. 7 John Egan: An early chance from a corner and had his head in his hands afterwards, which suggests he feels he could have done better. Defended well. 7 Nobel Mendy: Perhaps lucky to get away with a shirt pull on Havertz but defended well apart from that. 6 Elliot Stroud: Forced Raya into a smart stop with a dangerous delivery into the box. Struggled with the threat of Madueke. 5 Tim Iroegbunam: Worked hard to break up the Arsenal play and subbed late on. 6 Lucas Gourna-Douath: A real calming presence in the middle of the pitch for Hull. Shielded the back four but tired as Arsenal pushed for the win. 6 Mohamed-Ali Cho: Lots of runs behind the Arsenal backline, taken off in the second half. 6 Oli McBurnie: Battled all afternoon against the physically dominant Konsa and Gabriel. 6 Gelhardt (on 60, Cho): Introduced a threat down the right wing. 6 Norton-Cuffy: (on 61, Coyle): Booked after making his first tackle. Under a lot of pressure as faced with Eze. 6 Herrington: (on 69, Ajayi): Replaced Ajayi and Hull conceded soon after. 6 After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: Chelsea Women v Everton Women | Match | Official Site - Chelsea Football Club
content: With a defensive record only bettered by Chelsea in the WSL this season, the Blues knew we would be in for a tough afternoon against Everton even before the match had kicked off, and so it proved as we had to settle for a point at Stamford Bridge. After a cagey first half hour, Sandy Baltimore broke the deadlock when a small connection on the ball saw her steer home from a Lucy Bronze header back across goal. It felt like Chelsea were on our way, but when Bronze took an unfortunate touch from a looping ball in, the Toffees were back on level terms just four minutes later, and the teams went in at 1-1 at the break. Despite Everton not managing a shot on target during the match, the visitors made things really difficult for the Blues, reducing us to half-chances throughout. Their efforts were rewarded as they kept us from adding to the scoreline and took a point away from the Bridge. Sonia Bompastor made four alterations to her starting XI, swapping Veerle Buurman, Nathalie Bjorn and Sjoeke Nusken for Bronze, Kadeisha Buchanan and Erin Cuthbert. Lauren James had unfortunately been ruled out with a hamstring injury earlier in the week, and Wieke Kaptein came into the line-up in her place. The head coach had mentioned in her pre-match press conference that she expected the visitors to defend well, and that's exactly what happened in the opening stages of the game as the Toffees played in a compact formation as they attempted to negate our strengths. Our first real attempt came from one of Ellie Carpenter's trademark runs down the flank, and as she let fly with a shot, only a tiny deflection from the defender saw it bounce just wide of the right-hand post. Melvine Malard was next to go close with a header that was just off target, but the offside flag went up soon afterwards to confirm that it wouldn't have counted. It wasn't going to be easy to break Everton down, but the Blues were getting closer. After a superb one-two with Carpenter, Kaptein blasted her shot towards goal but had her attempt cleared off the line. Our opener came soon afterwards. After we took a short corner, Katie McCabe swung a cross into the back post to find the head of Bronze. The centre-back cushioned her header across the face of goal, allowing Baltimore to nod home with the slightest of touches. Yet the Toffees hit back when a looping cross from Yuka Momiki took an unfortunate touch off Bronze and deflected into the back of the net. Our number 22 almost cancelled out the own goal with a bullet header seven minutes before the break, but an impressive stop saw Everton goalkeeper Courtney Brosnan tip the attempt over the bar. After another tight opening to the second half, Bompastor made a double substitution after 55 minutes, introducing Nusken and Thompson for Baltimore and Kaptein. The clock ticked towards 70 and, other than a series of corners, the Blues were yet to put any real pressure on a resolute Everton defence. When the Blues were awarded a free-kick for a late challenge on Carpenter, McCabe took it short to Thompson just outside her, and the American laid the ball off to Walsh. The midfielder bent in a curling shot, but Brosnan was able to collect. That was the only real danger we caused in the second half as the statistics showed we fired 21 shots on goal but ended the match with only three big chances created. It was a frustrating day, but we will look to regain top spot when we face leaders Manchester City next weekend in the WSL. We drop to second in the table, two points behind leaders Manchester City, following their 5-0 win over West Ham United earlier today. We travel to Sweden to face Hacken in the Women's Champions League on Tuesday, with kick-off set for 5.45pm UK time. We will then back at Stamford Bridge for our top-of-the-table clash with Man City next Saturday. Tickets are still available and you can secure your place here. title: England v Wallabies prediction: Steve Borthwick's side to have 'just enough' to win as hosts pass 'acid test' for November block - Planet Rugby
content: Ben Earl (left) and Harry Wilson (right) will meet in England v Australia this weekend England and Australia are set to resume their storied rivalry this weekend, as both sides seek to land a sucker punch in the Nations Championship opener on Sunday. This feels a pivotal Test for both sides, as they look to show their recent improvements are no flash in the pan. England come into the upcoming block finally back to winning ways, after two victories against Fiji and Argentina, but before that had endured their worst-ever Six Nations campaign and lost to the Springboks in their July Nations Championship opener. The Wallabies, meanwhile, seem to have found a new lease of life under new boss Les Kiss, and they sit on a record of five wins from seven in his tenure. However, those two defeats have come in their most recent outings, falling to an aggregate loss of 93-40 against the All Blacks in the Bledisloe Cup Tests. But this is a chance for both sides to really lay down a marker moving into the rest of the Nations Championship, and a win for either side could really act as a catapult towards the top of their respective pools. England are currently fourth in the Northern Hemisphere table after three Tests, but a win on Sunday plus results elsewhere falling their way could move them up to the top of the tree. Australia are third in the Southern Hemisphere pool at the time of writing, but while they are unable to climb up any places, could close the gap on both the All Blacks and Springboks with a victory. The sides are not unfamiliar to each other, either, with them meeting for the third successive year at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham, with Australia winning in 2024 and England getting revenge in 2025. There are probably a lot of interesting mini-battles within this game. England’s power game got them over the line against the Wallabies last year, while Australia’s desire to play out wide helped them to victory in 2024. England team: Winners and losers as Steve Borthwick ‘puts faith’ in forward pair while head coach ‘misses opportunity’ with returning duo’s omission This time around, though, it feels like the breakdown is going to be the main differential. Australia’s defensive system is almost built around being able to compete at the ruck, often leaving at least one for their back-rowers floating around the tackle to clamp down on the ball and win a turnover. It’s also the sheer speed of how messers Fraser McReight and Harry Wilson can get there that should worry England the most. But Steve Borthwick isn’t short of top breakdown operators either. His selection of Ben Curry at open side is a clear indication he will target this area, while Ben Earl, Maro Itoje and even replacement Henry Pollock are top operators in it as well. The breakdown is going to be a fascinating sub-plot to this contest. ﻿ Speaking ahead of the game, England boss Borthwick outlined his side are fully aware of the challenge ahead of them this weekend: “Australia are a talented side who have played a significant amount of Test rugby in recent months. We know the challenge that awaits us and we’re looking forward to it. “We’re excited to be playing in front of our home supporters and to start an important block of games. This will also be our last opportunity to face southern hemisphere opposition at home before the World Cup next year.” England have also named one potential debutant on the bench in the form of Greg Fisilau, and Borthwick explained what he coud bring to their side. “We’re all absolutely delighted for Greg,” he said. “He’s worked incredibly hard to get to this point and has earned his opportunity through the way he’s performed for Exeter and in our training environment. “He’s a powerful, athletic player who brings real energy to the team.” Kiss was equally as wary of his side’s opposition this weekend, saying: “The entire squad has travelled well and prepared with fantastic energy and excitement heading into this weekend. “Playing England on their home turf – at an iconic venue like Twickenham – is a massive challenge and another great opportunity for us to test ourselves against world-class opposition and keep building our game.” The importance of having Fin Smith coming through this week good to go cannot be overstated for England. The 24-year-old is firmly establishing himself as Borthwick’s go-to fly-half at the moment, with the rest of the attack and the starting backline seemingly built around him. His desire sit just that little bit deeper away from the front line really seems to work within this Lee Blackett system, allowing him to scan across the park and identify space to then send the game breakers through. He is also more than comfortable taking the line on himself and then playing flat to it, which only adds to his game and England’s shape. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Wing duo Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Tommy Freeman will also likely have a major impact on proceedings. While slightly different types of wingers, they both give England’s attack genuine power and pace, all while floating in and around play to just get their hands on the ball. They are also both supreme finishers when given a sniff of the line, which is crucial at this level. England will also likely lean on number eight Ben Earl to help lay the foundations in the tight. As he has so often proved in pretty much the entirety of Borthwick’s tenure as head coach, Earl is England’s chief battering ram up front with his willingness to carry and ability to break through the gainline almost at will, but he also acts as a key strike option in counter-attack play, as if he’s an extra centre when England are given broken field. His ability to slot into midfield is also a big tick in his box, with Borthwick returning to a 6-2 split on the bench. Australia also come into this one with an exciting wing duo of their own, in the form of Max Jorgensen and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii. In a similar way to England’s pairing, these two offer a really different set of skills to this Wallaby attack. Jorgensen’s pace makes him a real danger in broken field, while Suaalii’s shift out wide not only sees him given that sort of freedom to float around the pitch and allows Australia to tap into his aerial prowess too. It could have a huge effect on the Wallabies’ attack, if used correctly. Len Ikitau’s return to the side is also a huge boost for Kiss. His injuries have meant we’ve only seen flashes of his quality this year in the Gold jersey, but those have been nothing short of brilliant. He was arguably the best player on the pitch before his knock against the Springboks, and added some nice flicks against Los Pumas as well. His blend of silky handling and genuine grunt in the carry make him an all-round threat, and that should make him a prominent part of the attack this weekend. Ryan Lonergan is also becoming a major player for the Wallabies in their recent run. He just seems to add a real layer of control and calmness to their play from the base of the ruck, almost in that French-style mould, and he should take a lot of the load of new fly-half Declan Meredith in the process. His goal-kicking is also top-notch, which is only a good thing at Test level. Lukhan Salakaia-Loto has been dipped in and out of the side in recent years, but he seems Kiss trusts him to go around and act as their chief enforcer. And it only brings the best out of him. The hulking forward relishes the ugly work in the tight, where he can smash and bash through the opposition. We’re cheating slightly here, but the battle of the back-row units is too good to ignore or pick just one from. It almost seems they perfectly match one another, too. At eight, Harry Wilson and Ben Earl will simply cart around for fun ball-in-hand, acting as their side’s chief ball carriers in the tight and helping set the tone for the rest of their pack in the process. At openside, Fraser McReight and Ben Curry will likely go toe-to-toe in the breakdown as they are tasked with trying to outdo the other and give their team the upper hand along the way. Interestingly, both coaches have opted for a hybrid at blindside, with the Wallabies shifting Jeremy Williams to blindside and Ollie Chessum continuing his back-row run for England too. This is clearly a move that gives them a big bopper to balance things out in that unit to free up their flanking partner, but also adds an extra option at the lineout as well. With the teams matching each other and the back-rows looking almost identical in their making, it will simply come down to whoever wants it more on the day. And that is an even more mouthwatering prospect. There is a lot of chatter, talk, noise, whatever you want to call it, surrounding this Test on Sunday, but England should pass this acid test. Ireland v Argentina: Five takeaways as ‘outstanding’ Hugo Keenan shines to leave ‘harsh truth’ for Felipe Contepomi Look, the noise, chatter, talk (nerves?) are not baseless. Australia are a team on the up once again and on a run of five wins from seven under new boss Kiss, including the scalp of the Springboks in that time. England are back in the winners column themselves, but you feel they need a properly convincing one to push their way back to the top table. And what better time to do that than this weekend, on home soil, in front of a packed-out Allianz Stadium. In the here and now, our money is on England to edge it. title: Hamilton v Leclerc: how can Ferrari solve problem of two number one drivers? - The Guardian
content: The Scuderia are hopeful of being in the world championship mix next season but risk puncturing their chances if they can’t corral their men in the cockpits Going into this weekend’s São Paulo Grand Prix, all indications are that the status quo at Ferrari will no longer suffice for Lewis Hamilton if the Scuderia’s ambition to return their first drivers’ Formula One championship since 2007 is to be taken seriously. This year’s drivers’ title is already decided with Kimi Antonelli triumphant at the last round in Mexico and Ferrari are looking towards next season where they are hopeful of genuinely being in the mix against the Italian and Mercedes. However, after Hamilton and his teammate Charles Leclerc clashed at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, the Briton clearly believes that a title tilt in 2027 might be at risk, as the team apparently vacillate on how to manage having two No 1 drivers, both determined to be the top dog around which Ferrari should coalesce. In Mexico, with Leclerc attempting to pass Hamilton, the move cost them both, Leclerc with a penalty and Hamilton in going wide and being passed by Max Verstappen who went on to win. The outcome denied Ferrari what would have been a likely victory and potentially a one-two. The team principal, Fred Vasseur, condemned the incident as demonstrating a lack of respect for the team and was expected to hold a crunch meeting with them both at Interlagos on Friday. It was not the first time this season the two Ferrari drivers have been uncompromising with one another. At Zandvoort Hamilton was frustrated when, on a different tyre strategy, Leclerc did not pit when first instructed to do so by the team in order to let the British driver past. A race later at Monza, Hamilton went down the inside of Leclerc into the first chicane and was squeezed wide by his teammate into the gravel. The notable difference after Mexico was Hamilton’s reaction. Previously he has been politic in stating they would deal with incidents behind closed doors – “offline” as he refers to it. After Mexico he publicly criticised Leclerc and before the race in Brazil was more bullish, refusing to be silenced in his criticism and making his position clear. “Naturally it’s not so easy having someone like me come into a team because I’m very outspoken,” he said. “I push and push and push for so many changes and I’m going to be pushing for more and as long as I’m here that’s how it’s going to be. I’m here to win.” That he is talking about it publicly indicates the seriousness of the situation. The team have no formal rules of engagement between the two and pointedly neither is considered the top driver in the way that Verstappen is at Red Bull. Last year with the team struggling it was irrelevant. This year the problem has been brought sharply into focus. With a title at stake in the future it could be the difference between winning and losing but this is far from a straightforward situation. Hamilton came to Ferrari on the back of enjoying de facto No 1 status at Mercedes, pretty much since Nico Rosberg retired after thein 2016 season. Leclerc, who is no less competitive, has enjoyed similar pre-eminence at Ferrari, with whom he has forged a strong relationship since he joined in 2019 and was long the favoured choice as their expected next champion. The complex demands and the fallout from letting them battle for dominance is far from new, as seen with Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost and Nigel Mansell and Nelson Piquet. Hamilton also knows about it, not least after his acrimonious fight with Rosberg in 2016. The latter was such that Mercedes, having been at pains to allow their drivers to race, had to impose rules of engagement. Vasseur has been painstaking so far in avoiding that scenario but he was left enormously frustrated after the incident in Mexico and knows how costly it could be. His is a very delicate balancing act however. McLaren had a similar problem with Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris in 2024 and 2025, and their efforts to allow their drivers to race without favour but also in managing them to the team’s advantage led to the adoption of their torturously complex “papaya rules”. These were satisfying to neither drivers nor fans, and did not appear particularly edifying to the team themselves. Notably however they did come out of it with the constructors’ title in 2024 and the double in 2025, a result that will not be lost on Ferrari. It has largely not been a problem for McLaren this season, with Norris enjoying a distinct advantage over his Australian teammate, of which Hamilton and Leclerc are aware. Both are determined to make themselves the focal point of the team; both are aware how important that is if the title is at stake. This has led to another fundamental problem for Ferrari. By not intervening in the process, they have seen the trust between the pair seemingly stretched to breaking point. Perhaps, it feels, within a whisker of becoming actively counterproductive from which a further, more damaging deterioration threatens. As Hamilton appears to be now insisting, Ferrari must address the issue but Leclerc cannot be faulted for simply following his instincts as a competitor. Both drivers are committed to the team but both are as equally determined to win, ambitions that match those of the Scuderia, which if they are to be met they must surely now look to manage. In first practice at Interlagos, McLaren’s Norris topped the timesheets in front of the new champion Antonelli in second, with Verstappen third and Hamilton fourth. In the afternoon Antonelli was on top, from Norris and Verstappen with Mercedes’ George Russell in fourth. Russell is, however, set to take a five-place grid penalty on Sunday for using a new engine in Brazil. Hamilton and Leclerc were in sixth and seventh. title: We Took a Cadillac XLR-V Onto Europe’s Most Challenging Roads, and It Delivered - MotorTrend
content: We tackled some of Europe’s fastest and most challenging roads in a Cadillac. [This story originally appeared in the January 2008 issue of Motor Trend with the headline "A Long Way From Motown," and comes from a time when we had a space in our name.] The Porsches don’t want to play. Over 1000 hard-charging miles in two days across Germany, Austria, and Italy, and not one appears in the Cadillac’s sights. Which is a pity, because our wedgy, quad-piped XLR-V is locked and loaded for 911s. Whoa! Back up a minute! Did I just say we went chasing Porsches … in a Cadillac? In Germany? Um, yeah. Because that’s exactly what we did. And while the 911s proved elusive, no one—apart from a lunatic in a black BMW 645i convertible who kept the hammer down in a speed-limited construction zone—passed our XLR-V on the autobahnen. Not the silver-haired guy in the big, black Audi S8 with Wuppertal plates. Nor the guy in the E46 M3 who tried to run with us near Nuremberg. Nor even the guy in the AMG Benz who gave us a cold, hard stare after we blew by him near Mainz. They couldn’t keep up. Cadillac general manager Jim Taylor clearly has a sense of adventure, because when I idly suggested a while back it might be fun to disable the 155-mph speed limiter on an XLR-V and take it to Germany to see what it would do on highways with no speed limits, he didn’t suddenly look at his watch and start mumbling something about a meeting he had to catch. Instead, he simply cracked a wry grin: “That sounds like fun. Let me see what I can do.” Third gear is stunning, giving you an effective operating range of 37 to 129 mph. Lord only knows what it took to shepherd the idea through GM; every few months I’d see Taylor at some event or other and he’d always say, “I haven’t forgotten.” But Cadillac’s decision to hold preview drives of the all-new CTS sedan at the Nürburgring made a bunch of logistics a whole lot easier, which is how photographer Mark Bramley and I came to be pulling out of the car park of the Hyatt Regency Hotel in Mainz, Germany, bound for Italy and the famed Stelvio Pass in an Infrared metallic XLR-V. Why the Stelvio Pass? Well, as British mountaineer George Leigh Mallory explained when asked in 1923 why he wanted to climb Mt. Everest: “Because it’s there.” Located where Switzerland kisses Italy and Austria, the 9045-foot Stelvio is the second-highest paved pass in the Alps. Originally built in the 1820s, and little changed since, it reaches a one-in-nine gradient at some points and features 48 hairpins on the northern side. The view of the road writhing down the ancient glacial valley is one of the most iconic in motoring. “Our” XLR-V was stock apart from a simple change to the engine-management computer that banished the speed nanny to the electronic ether. GM also took the precaution of X-raying the wheels and tires for any cracks or faults, though if you think about it, you’re not going to be in that much more trouble if a tire pops at 170 mph or so than if it does at the regulation 155. Still, it’s nice to know they care. Contrary to popular legend, Germany’s autobahnen aren’t pedal-to-the-metal paradises where you can run as fast as you dare, as long as you like. Germany is slightly smaller than Montana, but has a population of more than 80 million people. So many of the country’s superhighways often look like rush hour in L.A., clogged with slow-moving cars and trucks. The natural gait of the XLR-V is somewhere between 135 and 140 mph. We take the long way out of Mainz to avoid the worst of the congestion, driving west, then south, before swinging east to cross the Rhine and head toward Heidelberg. Just as we turn east, where the A61 meets the A6, we bust the second autobahn myth: There are speed limits, and they’re ruthlessly enforced. Wheeling around a long on-ramp, something flashes in my peripheral vision, and as we clear the corner there’s a German police car, blue lights flashing along with a “Follow Me” sign—helpfully in English and French, as well as in German. He leads us into a nearby rest area where we join an orderly line of fellow drivers, licenses and wallets in hand, standing outside a Mercedes van. A guardrail-mounted speed camera has nailed the XLR-V at 80 mph in a 60 zone. As we wait, Bramley says Germany’s started to crack down hard on speeding drivers and warns me this could be expensive. As it turns out, there’s a sliding scale of fines, and foreigners get off a lot more lightly than do Germans. The cop relieves me of 95 euro—about $130. “For you, it’s cheap,” he smiles. Transaction over, we walk back to the car. I’m just about to fire up the supercharged V-8 when I see the cop striding toward us. Uh-oh, here comes the lecture. I roll down the window. The cop reaches into his pocket, pulls out a packet of cigarettes, and eyes the Michigan-plated Caddy, the brash Yank on a European vacation. Suddenly, he grins: “Now, I must say this: Gentlemen, start your engines!” Then he throws back his head, and roars with laughter. A German traffic cop with a sense of humor. Now I’ve seen everything. Back on the road, and clear of speed limits, we loaf along at 100 mph or so until the traffic clears and I can nail the gas. There’s a momentary lull as the six-speed auto shuffles back a couple ratios, then the Northstar growls into action. I see 168 mph on the head-up display (the speedo runs only to 160) before the traffic builds again, and I’m forced to back off. Analog speedo tops out at 160 mph, but we saw 171 mph on the head-up digital display. We cruise as fast as the traffic allows down to the Austrian border. The XLR-V’s natural gait is somewhere between 135 and 140 mph—a relatively restrained 2800 to 3000 rpm in the moonshot sixth gear. At these speeds it feels as comfortable, relaxed, and stable as an SL, though there’s much more wind noise from around the roof than in the Mercedes. Bramley no stranger to fast and exotic European machinery, raises an approving eyebrow. “It’s better than I thought it would be,” he says. The Cadillac is far from a Benz rival in other ways, though—you need only one glance around the cabin, taking in the cheap-looking plastics, old-school switchgear, and low-rent graphics to see that. The ergonomics could be better, too: The seat cushion is too short, and the pedals too high and vertical. You’d never guess GM once led the world in the study of biomechanics. It’s late afternoon by the time we reach Italy and the north side of the Stelvio. The XLR-V has proven surprisingly quick and agile on the smooth mountain roads, reminding me a lot—and, yes, I’m surprised to find myself writing this—of our Jaguar XKR long-termer. The Cadillac has that same fast yet relaxed feel of the Jag, although the British car steers more crisply, rides better, brakes harder, and feels much more rigidly constructed. Still, there’s the genesis of a great GT in this Cadillac. All GM has to do is sweat the details. The 443-horsepower, supercharged Northstar V-8 is a gem, smooth and flexible and willing to rev, with a solid side order of torque on hand whenever you need it. I move the shift lever across the gate into manual mode, working through second, third, and fourth as we zigzag through the hills. Third gear is stunning—the V-8 pulls like a train from 2000 rpm and doesn’t stop until it nudges 6700, giving you an effective operating range of 37 to 129 mph. The Caddy demolishes short straightaways and barely draws breath up the hills, the V-8 exhaust note booming off the rock walls. The Stelvio itself is astonishing. The road climbs steadily through the forest, switchbacks here and there, before we break through the treeline. Then the hairpins pile one on top of the other; in places the road doubles back on itself two or three times in the space of a few hundred yards. Traffic’s light—most of the bikers who swarm over the place on summer weekends are already in their hotels enjoying an early evening beer—so I can push a little, punching hard out of the hairpins in first gear, snick-snicking into second, then third, before getting hard on the brakes, and double-pumping the shift lever to grab first again for another hairpin. Even with power steering and no clutch pedal, climbing the Stelvio is a physical business. We check into one of the hotels at the very top of the pass. Just down the hill, on the southern side, is the Swiss border. We drive down and cross over, just for the hell of it: It’s not often you get to drive through four countries in one day. Especially in a Cadillac. The next morning dawns bright and clear, so we’re up before breakfast, working the photo ops on the north side of the pass. By the time we finish, it’s past 9 a.m., and Bramley’s due on a 6 p.m. plane out of Frankfurt, more than 500 miles away. I look at the maps and decide we’ll cut east to pick up the autostrada at Merano and drive south to join the A22, which will take us up and over the Brenner Pass back into Austria. It’s going to be a hard slog. The XLR-V draws lots of stares from the car-savvy Italians as we stalk through the shoals of Fiats and Fords on the Brenner Pass. Cadillac’s distinctive visual signature—confident, powerful, chiseled—stands out among the Euro-chic background noise. As with the mechanical package, there’s a world-beating car lurking here, but GM needs to improve panel fit and paint finish (I’ve seen runs along the edge of an XLR-V hood) and finesse the jewelry. The traffic’s heavy, but flowing briskly, and the run down from the top of the Brenner Pass toward Innsbruck gives us the best gas mileage of the trip, 20.5 mpg at an average of 61 mph. But our hopes of making good time to Frankfurt are dashed by a traffic jam just inside the German border, south of Munich. I check the sat nav to find a back road off the autobahn at the next exit, but by the time we wind through a host of picturesque villages and get back onto the A8, we’ve probably burned an hour. We skirt around the east side of Munich and head north, back toward Nuremberg. The traffic clears, and we can run 125-130 mph for a bit. But only a bit—one minute the trip computer says we have 40 miles’ worth of gas left, next we’re running on fumes. I soft-pedal it into a gas station near Nuremberg and pump 15.8 gallons into the tank. We’re struggling to get much more than 250 miles between fuel stops. Memo, Cadillac: A 20-gallon tank would be nice. We make Frankfurt just in time, and I head back to Mainz after dropping Bramley at Departures, looping around to get to a quiet autobahn on the other side of the city. I’m still looking for Porsches. And room to top 168 mph. The A63 is near empty, and unrestricted. Perfect. I settle back in the seat and nail the gas. The Northstar growls, the induction roar ratcheting up an octave as the tach needle swings past 3600 rpm. First gear runs to 47 mph, second to 80, third 124, and fourth hits 165. The transmission slips into fifth, and the digital display keeps ticking off the increments, more slowly now. 169…170…171 mph. And that’s it, not the least because I’ve just chewed through a quarter tank of gas in less than 15 minutes, and I have to find a gas station again. Okay, I didn’t get to surprise any 911s. But I did learn one thing: There’s no reason why Cadillac can’t build a world-beating GT. The XLR-V’s far from perfect, but it’s a lot more at home in Europe than you might think. title: Verdict: Is the Acura ADX Just a Luxurious Honda HR-V? Yes, but That’s a Good Thing - MotorTrend
content: Acura builds a surprisingly satisfying luxury experience on a mainstream foundation. Dreams often clash with reality. Indulging in a luxury vehicle can bring style, performance, refinement, and—perhaps most important—the pride of knowing you’ve made it, that you got something better than a simple transportation appliance. At the same time, it can introduce practical perils. Think uncertain reliability, fussy interfaces, and design that compromises function for form. Over 13 months spent driving our yearlong review 2025 Acura ADX, our Acura succeeded in balancing those considerations. How it manages that balancing act will appeal greatly to some drivers and make others steer away. Here’s the rub: The ADX is just so similar to the Honda HR-V. Their dimensions, hardware, interior, features, and even paint are very alike, if not identical. Acuras always use Honda parts but typically try at least a little harder to hide those under a premium veneer. Few subcompact luxury SUV rivals share so much with a mainstream vehicle. That’s a valid concern for drivers who seek badge cachet and want their vehicle to project status in traffic. But otherwise? Not a problem, in my opinion. Honda builds practical, sensible, reliable vehicles with strong value. They tend to drive nicely, too. With that, the HR-V appeals as a normal little crossover that’s easy to use and live with. If that’s the baseline need but there’s a desire for something nicer, something more, then the ADX could be just the thing. Think of it like a luxury trim package for the HR-V, and the ADX starts to make sense. I held that frame of reference during my time with the ADX, and in that, I remained satisfied. The ADX made an adept daily driver. It’s small and easy to park, yet it’s spacious enough to fit my extra-tall self and, with the second-row seats folded, my accordingly tall custom-made bicycle without removing the wheels. It has a bunch of real buttons, which are shared with the HR-V but actuate with a nice tactile feel. In a time when fussy digital controls infest so many cars, these easy-to-use manual knobs and air vents felt like luxury in themselves. Likewise, the familiarity of unlocking with a key, pushing the starter, throwing the shifter into drive, and heading off shouldn’t be underestimated these days. This relative simplicity invites comparison to the HR-V; none of it is particularly high-tech or design-forward. Yet our high-end A-Spec model with the Advance package had touches that elevate it from its Honda basis. The off-white Orchid perforated leather with blue microsuede accents made an appealing combination, and the light upholstery resisted discoloration. The heated and ventilated front seats and heated steering wheel got plenty warm and cool. (More details in our 2025 Acura ADX interior review.) A button on the turn signal stalk activated the 360-degree camera, which became indispensable when parking and maneuvering in tight spaces. The 15-speaker Bang & Olufsen audio system sounds really good, too. For tech, the ADX borrows from the Honda parts bin. Its 10.2-inch digital gauge display looks fine and displays necessary information, but it lacks the reconfigurability and cool graphics seen in some rivals. Likewise, the 9.0-inch infotainment touchscreen had a straightforward user interface, but it’s neither as sharp nor as large as those in competitors. That said, the addition of the Google Gemini AI voice assistant midway through the loan proved to be a useful upgrade. Overall, it’s enough tech but might not impress those who equate huge screens with luxury. The ADX’s reliability and dependability upheld its maker’s reputation. It had no unexpected issues or faults whatsoever. The one scheduled service visit at about 11,000 miles included basics such as an oil change, tire rotation, and inspection of various systems. Although we paid out of pocket due to a stipulation of how Acura allocates test vehicles to media, actual Acura buyers get scheduled maintenance covered during the first 12 months or 12,000 miles of ownership. Beyond that period, owners might anticipate paying the $430.24 we did. Over the 18,652 miles we drove, the ADX averaged 25.4 mpg, reasonably close to its 27-mpg EPA combined fuel economy rating. Cost per mile came to $0.23, reasonable in the context of today’s egregious gas prices; a hybrid ADX would be a welcome addition. The closest comparison from our long-term fleet would be the 2022 Toyota Corolla Cross, another subcompact SUV, which itself underpins a luxury vehicle, the rival Lexus UX. Over its nearly 17,000-mile service life, the Corolla Cross got 29.0 mpg average at a cost per mile of $0.17. Our recently departed 2025 Acura Integra Type S also has a turbocharged I-4 engine and averaged 23.6 mpg at $0.23 per mile over 15,400 miles, not bad considering how hard we drove it. One fueling foible relates to the ADX’s gas tank size. Even though driving range is rated at 378 miles, the most we ever got from a tank was 345 miles—20 miles past the vehicle displaying zero range remaining. Oddly, the fuel gauge shows empty when there are actually two gallons left in the tank, an unnecessarily large buffer. On the plus side, the capless fuel filler is a nice convenience. Some things about the ADX irked me. Wireless Apple CarPlay connectivity was spotty; it usually connected instantly, but occasionally I’d need to select my iPhone from the touchscreen. However, after Gemini and its upgraded Google Maps capability arrived, I basically stopped using CarPlay. The passenger-side mirror tilts down in reverse but wouldn’t always rise back up to exactly where I’d set it. Most annoying was the terrible adaptive cruise control. It was extremely slow to respond to traffic ahead, sometimes taking several seconds to detect a braking vehicle. I’d see taillights illuminate then count to three or four before it reacted abruptly. This feature works better in every other Acura and Honda I’ve tried, making its application in our ADX seem like an unfortunate fluke. Whenever I drove myself, though, I enjoyed the ADX’s connected dynamics. Its 190-hp, 179 lb-ft 1.5-liter turbocharged I-4 and CVT automatic produced an objectively slow-for-its-segment 8.9-second 0–60-mph time, and wide-open acceleration was accompanied by a coarse soundtrack. But that was rarely needed. Torque arrives promptly, making the little engine feel stronger than its numbers suggest. The CVT was free of the rubber-band sensations other transmissions of this type can display, and its paddle shifters helped sharpen response in traffic or before a merge, providing a surprising degree of control. Direct, hefty steering and a firm, responsive brake pedal contributed to the almost sporty feel. Suspension tuning nicely balanced poise in corners and long-distance comfort. Road noise was fairly pervasive, though, detracting from the luxury credentials. Maybe that’s acceptable given the price. At under $46,000 fully loaded, the ADX tops out near where some rivals begin. Equipped to match the ADX, they easily cost thousands more. That makes the ADX a value play in the segment. Then again, it’s largely a luxed-up Honda HR-V with a stronger engine. It’s still somewhat loud, unsophisticated, and not especially distinctive. Even if you see panache in the Acura badge, accepting those similarities could be a reach. But as other upmarket automakers stuff their entry-level SUVs with dazzling doodads, annoying add-ons, and poseurish performance packages, the ADX takes a more predictable direction. That could appeal if you want to avoid the potential complications that come from owning an SUV from Acura’s competitors. The ADX isn’t dramatically better than an HR-V. Rather, it makes its case by being nicer in little ways. Here, any concern around the Honda connection comes down to perspective. It’s either too close to what everyone else drives or a strong basis for easy ownership. During my time with the ADX, I drove vehicles that put more emphasis on cutting-edge design, driver involvement, or absolute refinement. But returning to the ADX was always refreshing. Even if it never wowed me, it also never made me think twice about getting where I needed to go or doing what I needed to do. It just worked. And the extra layer of Acura polish smoothed out the daily grind. Is that the stuff of dreams? Perhaps not. That’s fine—the Acura ADX is built for reality. title: Daniel V. Hickey Obituary Nov 6, 2026 - Olson Funeral Home - Bloomer
content:
Daniel V. Hickey, age 86, of New Auburn, passed away peacefully on Friday, November 6, 2026, at Dove Rutledge Home in Chippewa Falls, under the care of Lily Hospice. Dan was born on March 24, 1940, in Tomahawk, WI to Vernon and Helen (Mason) Hickey. He attended Rhinelander High School and graduated with the Class of 1958. On December 27, 1986, Dan married Connie Demick in Bloomer, WI. He proudly served in the United States Marine Corps. After his service, Dan attended college at UW-Milwaukee where he ran track and earned a degree in physical education and geography. Upon graduation, Dan pursued an international career that took him to many places including Taipei, Taiwan and Cairo, Egypt, where he served as teacher, coach, athletic director and administrator. Upon return from overseas, Dan settled in New Auburn in 1979. He served as principal, then superintendent for the New Auburn School District for over 20 years. Additionally, Dan founded the New Auburn Syndrome Rugby Club where many people got to know him as a teammate, coach and mentor. Dan was a lifelong athlete, passionate about martial arts and rugby. Dan enjoyed sharing his passion for athletics with others, always bringing the same enthusiasm and commitment to every team and student. Upon retirement, Dan coached the UW–Stout Girls Rugby Team. He also had a keen interest in collecting firearms. Dan is survived by his wife: Connie Hickey; four children: Heather (Dan) Matthews of Florida, Kimberly Hickey of South Carolina, Don (Karen) Demick of Madison and John (Kerri) Hickey of Germantown; siblings: Patricia Donkle of Cambridge; five grandchildren; and numerous nieces, nephews, other relatives and friends.
